nodes.title: Two-party private computation becomes a general protocol problem
nodes.subtitle: Protocols for Secure Computations
nodes.summary: Yao formulates and gives protocols for two parties to compute functions of private inputs while limiting what each party learns, establishing secure two-party computation as a general cryptographic task.

metadata.title: Two-party private computation becomes a general protocol problem
metadata.statement: Yao formulates and gives protocols for two parties to compute functions of private inputs while limiting what each party learns, establishing secure two-party computation as a general cryptographic task.

historical_context.prior_boundary: Cryptographic protocols protected communication or solved specialized coordination tasks, but there was no comparably general protocol formulation for computing on two parties' private data.
historical_context.technical_delta: The paper treats private function evaluation itself as the object to construct and presents protocols that separate the desired output from the parties' hidden inputs.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: It supplied the problem boundary from which general secure-computation compilers and the garbled-circuit tradition could be developed.
historical_context.narrative: Earlier cryptographic protocols protected messages or addressed particular coordination problems, but they did not yet provide a general language for two parties computing on private inputs. Yao made the computation itself the cryptographic object: specify a function, let each party retain its input, and reveal only the prescribed result within the protocol's security model. The contribution is this general secure two-party computation paradigm and its protocol feasibility, not every detail later associated with modern garbled circuits. At publication time it created a common problem statement against which later circuit compilers, garbling techniques, oblivious-transfer optimizations, and concrete systems could be compared.

source_locator.primary_source: Abstract and protocol constructions

limitations: the record does not attribute every modern garbled-circuit formalization to this paper
the exact security formulation predates contemporary simulation frameworks

sections.heading: Main claims
sections.content: When at least half of the parties may be corrupted, in any r-round coin-flipping protocol the corrupted parties can bias the honest parties' output by \( \Omega(1/r) \). In particular, complete fairness is impossible in general without an honest majority.

sections.heading: Historical role
sections.content: It sets the lower bound that optimally fair coin flipping for three or more parties asks to match, and it is the starting point for characterizing fair two-party functions.

nodes.title: Circuit compilation gives general MPC with explicit adversary upgrades
nodes.subtitle: How to Play ANY Mental Game
nodes.summary: Goldreich, Micali, and Wigderson give a general circuit-based method for secure multiparty computation and separate passive evaluation from compilation techniques that enforce security against stronger adversarial behavior.

metadata.title: Circuit compilation gives general MPC with explicit adversary upgrades
metadata.statement: Goldreich, Micali, and Wigderson give a general circuit-based method for secure multiparty computation and separate passive evaluation from compilation techniques that enforce security against stronger adversarial behavior.

historical_context.prior_boundary: Secure computation was represented by early two-party protocols and specialized tasks rather than a general compiler from arbitrary polynomial-time functionality to a secure multiparty protocol.
historical_context.technical_delta: GMW reduces general computation to secure instruction-by-instruction evaluation of a program derived from the circuit and organizes the treatment of passive and malicious behavior through distinct protocol and compilation steps.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: It established generality as a theorem-level MPC boundary and made adversary handling an explicit layer rather than an informal property of one protocol.
historical_context.narrative: Early secure-computation results showed that privacy-preserving interaction was possible, but did not yet provide a uniform recipe for arbitrary multiparty functionalities under clearly separated adversary models. GMW turns the target computation into a circuit-derived program, evaluates it on distributed values, and distinguishes the machinery needed for passive execution from the additional enforcement required against malicious behavior. The atomic change is a general compilation architecture, not a single optimized gate protocol. This mattered because subsequent MPC research could improve sharing, oblivious transfer, consistency checks, or setup while retaining a recognizable completeness contract for general computation.

source_locator.primary_source: ACM book reprint (2019, Chapter 13) of STOC 1987 pp. 218–229, chapter page numbers; §2.3 (p. 311), §4 Theorem (p. 314), §4.1–§4.3 (pp. 314–322), §5 (pp. 322–323), §6.4 (p. 327)

qualifiers: Polynomial-time functionalities given as Turing machines and converted to circuits and then to Barrington straight-line programs over S5 (§4.3, p. 320).
The passive solver assumes trapdoor functions (§4, p. 314) and tolerates any number of passive adversaries (§2.3, p. 311).
Malicious security holds for fewer than n/2 malicious players who complete the engagement protocol, by zero-knowledge proofs of correct messages (§5, pp. 322–323).
limitations: The extended abstract sketches the passive construction with the adversarial set fixed at the start (§4, p. 314) and defers the malicious-case proof to the final paper (§5, p. 322).
Round and communication costs depend on the circuit and subprotocols; later frameworks refine the security and composition contract.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: GMW compiler The complete GMW protocol family remains a construction object; this record isolates the compiler-level research delta.

metadata.title: How to Play ANY Mental Game
versions: ACM book reprint 2019 as Chapter 13 of Providing Sound Foundations for Cryptography (DOI 10.1145/3335741.3335755; reading copy)

sections.heading: Role
sections.content: GMW is represented by its general Boolean secret-sharing configuration, not by every later optimized protocol carrying the name.

sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes
sections.content: The reading copy is the 2019 ACM book reprint: Chapter 13 of *Providing Sound Foundations for Cryptography: On the Work of Shafi Goldwasser and Silvio Micali* (DOI 10.1145/3335741.3335755). Its opening page states that the chapter reproduces the STOC 1987 paper, pp. 218–229. Locators use the chapter's printed page numbers (309–328); the opening page and the abstract page carry none. The opening page's summary paragraph is the book's editorial note, not part of the 1987 text. The author-hosted copy cited before 2026-10-11 was not re-read.

sections.heading: Atomic contribution
sections.content: MPC-CONTRIB-1987-GMW-COMPILER records the general compiler. The checked locators are the following. §2.3 (p. 311): all Turing-machine games are playable with any number of passive adversaries or with fewer than n/2 malicious ones. §4, Theorem (p. 314): a solver for passive adversaries exists if trapdoor functions exist. The sketch fixes the adversarial set at the start. §4.1 (pp. 314–318): a new one-out-of-two OT from any trapdoor permutation, secure against passive adversaries. §4.2 (pp. 318–320): Yao's combined oblivious transfer, built on that OT. §4.3 (pp. 320–322): the circuit is turned into a Barrington straight-line program over S5, whose instructions are evaluated on shares of permutations, using combined oblivious transfer for products of two variables. §5 (pp. 322–323): against fewer than n/2 malicious players, an engagement protocol (verifiable secret sharing and multi-party coin flipping) precedes the passive protocol. Each message is then proved correct in zero knowledge. The proof is deferred to the final paper. §6.4 (p. 327): the completeness theorem for fault-tolerant computation. The optimality remark for a dishonest majority is on p. 309. The XOR-sharing gate evaluation now usually called GMW is not the construction in this extended abstract. §7 (p. 327) mentions simpler later solvers by Haber and Micali and by Goldreich and Vainish.

sections.heading: Relations
sections.content: Yao: §4.2 (p. 318) credits Yao's [Y2] with the combined oblivious transfer protocol and strengthens its assumption from factoring to any trapdoor permutation. The reference list (p. 328) gives [Y2] as How to Generate and Exchange Secrets, 1986, pp. 162–167. Yao's [Y] (FOCS 1982, Theory and Application of Trapdoor Functions) is cited only for computational indistinguishability and random bits (pp. 312, 316). The chapter does not cite the mapped 1982 Yao paper, Protocols for Secure Computations. The 1986 paper has no card, so no Yao-to-GMW lineage edge is recorded. BGW names this paper as the main inspiration for its non-cryptographic completeness theorems. That relation is sourced from BGW's text (see lineage.yaml).

sections.heading: Limitations and unresolved review
sections.content: This review checks statements, models, and locators in an extended abstract whose malicious-case proof is deferred; it is not an independent verification of the proofs.

nodes.title: Honest-majority thresholds characterize information-theoretic general MPC
nodes.subtitle: Completeness Theorems for Non-Cryptographic Fault-Tolerant Distributed Computation
nodes.summary: BGW establishes unconditional general MPC over private channels for passive corruption below one half and Byzantine corruption below one third, together with matching threshold limitations in its model.

metadata.title: Honest-majority thresholds characterize information-theoretic general MPC
metadata.statement: BGW establishes unconditional general MPC over private channels for passive corruption below one half and Byzantine corruption below one third, together with matching threshold limitations in its model.

historical_context.prior_boundary: General secure computation was becoming possible under computational assumptions, but the exact unconditional feasibility frontier as a function of corruptions and communication assumptions was not yet settled.
historical_context.technical_delta: BGW combines polynomial secret sharing, degree reduction, and verifiable sharing to obtain general protocols at honest-majority thresholds and proves the corresponding model-specific limitations.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: It turned party threshold and adversary behavior into explicit feasibility coordinates and founded the arithmetic secret-sharing line of MPC.
historical_context.narrative: General MPC feasibility did not by itself answer whether cryptographic hardness was necessary or how many corrupt parties an information-theoretic protocol could tolerate. BGW uses polynomial sharing to represent values and compute arithmetic circuits, adding verifiability for Byzantine behavior. In the private-channel model, the resulting boundaries separate passive corruption below one half from active corruption below one third, with matching impossibility statements for the relevant thresholds. This was more than a new construction: it made corruption threshold and adversary behavior first-class coordinates of an MPC claim. The result anchored later honest-majority protocols, generalized sharing schemes, and comparisons between synchronous and asynchronous feasibility.

qualifiers: errorless privacy and correctness in the main protocols (p. 2)
limitations: thresholds are model-dependent

sections.heading: Boundary note

sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes
sections.content: The reading copy is the ACM Digital Library scan of the STOC 1988 extended abstract (DOI 10.1145/62212.62213). Its ten PDF pages match the printed proceedings pages 1–10. The text layer is OCR and partly garbled, so locators were checked against the page layout. The mirror cited before 2026-10-11 was not re-read.

sections.heading: Atomic contribution
sections.content: MPC-CONTRIB-1988-BGW-THRESHOLDS records the threshold frontier. The checked locators are the following. The abstract (p. 1) states the two thresholds and their tightness. The model is a complete synchronous network with secure pairwise channels (Definitions and Results, p. 2). Theorems 1–4 are stated on pp. 2–3. The proof of Theorem 1 (pp. 3–4) uses polynomial sharing, local linear operations, and a randomizing degree-reduction step. Its remarks (p. 5) bound rounds by circuit depth. Theorem 2, proved on p. 5, rests on the two-party OR function. Secret sharing with cheaters and secret verification, both with error and errorless, are on pp. 5–7. Theorem 3 is proved on p. 8. Theorem 4 (p. 9) follows from the Byzantine-agreement lower bound.

sections.heading: Relations
sections.content: GMW: the introduction (p. 1) names the multi-party completeness result [GMW2] as the main inspiration. Page 2 compares the thresholds with that cryptographic case. This sources the GMW-to-BGW edge in lineage.yaml. Chaum, Crépeau, and Damgård are credited with independently discovering essentially the same results (p. 2). That paper has no card.

sections.heading: Limitations and unresolved review
sections.content: Several proofs are omitted in the extended abstract. This review checks statements, models, and locators, not an independent verification of the proofs.

nodes.title: Distributed garbling removes circuit depth from MPC round complexity
nodes.subtitle: The Round Complexity of Secure Protocols
nodes.summary: Beaver, Micali, and Rogaway construct constant-round multiparty computation by distributing garbled-circuit preparation so that the online interaction does not grow with circuit depth.

metadata.title: Distributed garbling removes circuit depth from MPC round complexity
metadata.statement: Beaver, Micali, and Rogaway construct constant-round multiparty computation by distributing garbled-circuit preparation so that the online interaction does not grow with circuit depth.

historical_context.prior_boundary: Gate-by-gate circuit protocols naturally incurred interaction proportional to circuit depth, making round complexity a structural cost of general MPC.
historical_context.technical_delta: BMR has the parties jointly prepare a garbled representation whose later evaluation is predominantly local, separating communication rounds from the depth of the evaluated circuit.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: It opened distributed garbling as a distinct architecture and showed that depth-dependent rounds were not inherent to general secure computation.
historical_context.narrative: Circuit-based MPC was general, but evaluating shared gates in sequence tied interaction to circuit depth. BMR changes the execution architecture: parties cooperate to prepare a garbled circuit and then evaluate that representation without repeating an interactive protocol at every level. The resulting protocol achieves a constant number of rounds under its stated cryptographic model even when the circuit is deep. The contribution is this distributed-garbling route to round reduction, not a claim that communication or computation becomes constant. It mattered because later work could optimize the distributed preparation, strengthen it against malicious parties, or combine it with preprocessing while retaining the same low-round online structure.

nodes.subtitle: Efficient Multiparty Protocols Using Circuit Randomization
nodes.summary: Beaver's circuit-randomization method uses input-independent correlated multiplication values so arithmetic products can be opened and completed online with lightweight interaction once the correlations are available.

metadata.title: Input-independent multiplication triples separate MPC preprocessing from online work
metadata.statement: Beaver's circuit-randomization method uses input-independent correlated multiplication values so arithmetic products can be opened and completed online with lightweight interaction once the correlations are available.

historical_context.prior_boundary: Arithmetic MPC evaluated multiplication through interactive protocols whose expensive cryptographic work remained coupled to the parties' live inputs and circuit execution.
historical_context.technical_delta: Random triples satisfying a multiplicative relation are prepared independently of inputs and later mask the online multiplication, moving the hard work into a reusable offline phase.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: It supplied the enduring online/offline abstraction behind many arithmetic MPC protocols and made correlation generation an independent optimization target.
historical_context.narrative: Arithmetic sharing makes addition local, but multiplication normally forces the parties back into an interactive cryptographic subprotocol. Beaver's circuit randomization prepares correlated random values before the actual inputs are known. During execution, parties reveal only masked differences and combine them with the preprocessed correlation to obtain a sharing of the product. The atomic contribution is the input-independent multiplication correlation and the clean separation it creates between offline generation and online evaluation. This mattered because subsequent protocols could preserve a simple online phase while replacing the way triples are generated—using homomorphic encryption, oblivious transfer, pseudorandom generators, or specialized honest-majority techniques.

nodes.title: General MPC remains feasible with arbitrarily delayed messages
nodes.subtitle: Asynchronous Secure Computation
nodes.summary: Ben-Or, Canetti, and Goldreich establish general secure computation in a completely asynchronous private-channel network with optimal resilience below one third for fail-stop faults and below one fourth for Byzantine faults.

metadata.title: General MPC remains feasible with arbitrarily delayed messages
metadata.statement: Ben-Or, Canetti, and Goldreich establish general secure computation in a completely asynchronous private-channel network with optimal resilience below one third for fail-stop faults and below one fourth for Byzantine faults.

historical_context.prior_boundary: Classical completeness results assumed a synchronous progression in which missing messages could be interpreted through known rounds and timing bounds.
historical_context.technical_delta: The protocol replaces round-based coordination with asynchronous verifiable sharing, agreement, and online error correction, with separate optimal resilience bounds for fail-stop and Byzantine faults.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: It showed that network timing and fault behavior jointly determine the exact feasibility frontier rather than merely slowing a synchronous MPC protocol.
historical_context.narrative: Honest-majority MPC completeness had been established in synchronous networks, where rounds and delivery bounds help parties decide when to continue. An asynchronous network removes that signal: a delayed message is indistinguishable from a failed sender. Ben-Or, Canetti, and Goldreich combine asynchronous agreement, errorless verifiable sharing, and online error correction so a computation can finish without hearing from faulty parties. The exact frontier depends on fault behavior: fewer than one third of parties may fail-stop, whereas Byzantine faults must remain below one fourth in this errorless construction. The contribution is therefore a model-specific feasibility theorem, not merely a slower implementation of synchronous MPC, and its two resilience bounds should not be collapsed into one generic honest-majority label.

limitations: the two fault types have different optimal resilience bounds
later probabilistic-error protocols reach different Byzantine thresholds
the result is not a claim for arbitrary dishonest majorities

nodes.title: Periodic share refresh prevents mobile corruptions from accumulating secrets
nodes.subtitle: Proactive Secret Sharing or: How to Cope With Perpetual Leakage
nodes.summary: Proactive secret sharing periodically rerandomizes distributed shares without changing the protected secret, preventing an adversary that compromises different parties in different epochs from accumulating a reconstructing set.

metadata.title: Periodic share refresh prevents mobile corruptions from accumulating secrets
metadata.statement: Proactive secret sharing periodically rerandomizes distributed shares without changing the protected secret, preventing an adversary that compromises different parties in different epochs from accumulating a reconstructing set.

historical_context.prior_boundary: Threshold sharing protected a secret only while the adversary remained below the threshold over the lifetime of one fixed sharing; compromises could otherwise accumulate over time.
historical_context.technical_delta: Parties refresh their shares and erase obsolete state so exposure in one period does not combine with exposure from another period to reveal the secret.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: It introduced an epoch-based security mechanism for long-lived distributed state and separated mobile-adversary resilience from one-shot MPC correctness.
historical_context.narrative: A static threshold guarantee limits how many shares an adversary sees at one moment, but a long-lived service may face compromises of different machines over time. If shares never change, those exposures accumulate. Proactive secret sharing periodically replaces each party's share with a fresh one representing the same secret, while old state is discarded. The atomic contribution is this cross-epoch rerandomization mechanism and its mobile-adversary boundary, not a complete general-purpose MPC stack. It mattered because distributed cryptographic services could reason about a bounded number of corruptions per period rather than a single lifetime compromise set, and later proactive MPC could reuse the refresh abstraction.

nodes.summary: Canetti, Feige, Goldreich, and Naor use non-committing encryption to obtain computational MPC over insecure channels against adaptive corruptions of non-erasing parties under the paper's threshold and trapdoor assumptions.

metadata.title: Non-committing techniques secure MPC against execution-dependent corruptions
metadata.statement: Canetti, Feige, Goldreich, and Naor use non-committing encryption to obtain computational MPC over insecure channels against adaptive corruptions of non-erasing parties under the paper's threshold and trapdoor assumptions.

historical_context.prior_boundary: Adaptive MPC was known with secure channels or trusted erasures, but ordinary ciphertexts over insecure channels could bind a simulator before a later corruption exposed the sender's retained state.
historical_context.technical_delta: Non-committing encryption lets simulated ciphertexts be explained consistently after corruption; the principal construction handles fewer than one third adaptive corruptions of non-erasing parties, with a stated modification below one half.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The work separated corruption timing and erasure behavior from ordinary malicious security and supplied a cryptographic compiler for the insecure-channel setting.
historical_context.narrative: Adaptive security over insecure channels creates a simulation problem absent from static proofs: a ciphertext sent before corruption must later agree with every piece of state retained by the newly compromised sender. Earlier routes avoided that conflict with secure channels or trusted erasures. Canetti, Feige, Goldreich, and Naor introduce non-committing encryption, allowing simulated ciphertexts to be explained consistently only when a corruption occurs. Their main construction gives general computational MPC for non-erasing parties below the stated corruption threshold using common-domain trapdoor systems, with RSA and Diffie-Hellman instantiations. This is an adaptive-simulation compiler, not an epoch-based proactive refresh mechanism.

limitations: the principal theorem handles fewer than one-third corruptions and notes a modification below one half
the compiler inherits its secure-channel protocol and trapdoor assumptions
proactive mobile corruption is a distinct contract

metadata.statement: Cramer, Damgård, and Maurer construct general MPC from multiplicative linear secret-sharing schemes, extending polynomial-threshold sharing to access structures whose multiplication and robustness conditions are stated algebraically.

historical_context.prior_boundary: Arithmetic MPC constructions were closely tied to threshold polynomial sharing, so their access structures and multiplication arguments did not directly cover general monotone corruption patterns.
historical_context.technical_delta: The paper identifies multiplicativity in a linear secret-sharing scheme as the algebraic interface needed to lift secure circuit evaluation to general access structures.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: It separated the sharing representation from the MPC compiler and made access-structure generality a reusable construction coordinate.
historical_context.narrative: BGW-style arithmetic MPC used the multiplication structure of polynomial threshold sharing, but many trust policies are not captured by a single threshold. Cramer, Damgård, and Maurer recast the protocol around linear secret-sharing schemes and isolate multiplicativity as the property that permits shared products to be combined correctly. The resulting construction supports general access structures under the paper's stated conditions. The atomic contribution is this representation-level abstraction and compiler, not merely another threshold protocol. At publication time it clarified which algebraic feature of sharing powers general MPC and enabled later work to design, analyze, and optimize protocols against richer corruption structures.

metadata.title: Randomizing Polynomials: A New Representation with Applications to Round-Efficient Secure Computation

sections.heading: Overview

sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes
sections.content: Checked through the FOCS 2000 abstract (Technion research portal record) and the authors' DIMACS 2000 talk abstract on the same work. The full paper was not available on 2026-10-10, so theorem numbers are not recorded.

sections.heading: Main claims
sections.content: Every function can be represented by randomizing polynomials of degree three: polynomials in the input and fresh random inputs whose output distribution depends only on the function's value. The size of this representation is tied to the function's branching-program size, and degree two does not suffice for most functions. Secure evaluation of any function therefore reduces to secure evaluation of degree-three polynomials; the talk abstract states two-round protocols against coalitions below one third and three-round protocols below one half, with communication at most quadratic in branching-program size and a small one-sided error.

sections.heading: Historical role
sections.content: It settles constant-round information-theoretic MPC for log-space functions and is the starting point of the randomized-encoding route to the general question.

sections.heading: Limitations and unresolved review
sections.content: The encodings are polynomial only for functions with polynomial-size branching programs; for general circuits the cost grows exponentially with depth.

metadata.title: Environment-based simulation makes concurrent protocol composition explicit
metadata.statement: Canetti defines universally composable security through an external environment and proves a composition theorem that preserves protocol security when secure subroutines are replaced inside arbitrary surrounding executions.

historical_context.prior_boundary: Stand-alone simulation proofs did not automatically justify using a secure protocol concurrently or as a subroutine inside a larger system.
historical_context.technical_delta: The UC framework quantifies over an interactive environment and formalizes ideal-functionality replacement so composition follows from a theorem under explicit setup assumptions.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: It changed the contract attached to MPC security claims by separating stand-alone privacy from security that survives arbitrary protocol context.
historical_context.narrative: A stand-alone MPC proof compares one execution with an ideal process, but a real protocol may run concurrently with other sessions or serve as a component of a larger application. The UC framework places the execution inside an interactive environment and asks whether replacing a real subprotocol with its ideal functionality remains indistinguishable. Its composition theorem then licenses modular replacement under the framework's assumptions. The contribution is a security definition and composition contract, not a new gate-evaluation mechanism. It mattered because later MPC papers had to state whether their setup, corruption model, and simulator supported composable use rather than treating every simulation argument as interchangeable.

metadata.title: Symmetric-key OT extension expands a small public-key seed into many transfers
metadata.statement: IKNP extends a small number of base oblivious transfers into a large batch using primarily symmetric-key operations, reducing the public-key cost of OT-intensive secure computation.

historical_context.prior_boundary: Protocols that consumed one oblivious transfer per wire or correlation inherited a public-key operation cost that scaled with the full OT batch.
historical_context.technical_delta: IKNP uses a small base-OT seed and matrix-style symmetric-key expansion to generate many additional transfers with only inexpensive hash and pseudorandom operations per item.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: It made OT a scalable correlation source for Boolean MPC and shifted optimization attention from public-key count to batch expansion and consistency.
historical_context.narrative: Oblivious transfer was a powerful complete primitive for secure computation, but invoking a public-key protocol for every required transfer made OT-heavy designs expensive. IKNP performs only a small base set of such transfers and expands them into a much larger batch using symmetric-key operations and correlated bit matrices. The atomic contribution is the amortized OT-extension mechanism and its reduction in public-key work, not a complete MPC protocol. This mattered because Boolean sharing, garbled circuits, and later authenticated-bit preprocessing could treat large OT batches as a practical resource. Subsequent work could then strengthen malicious security or make expansion silent without changing the underlying role of OT as correlation infrastructure.

limitations: security inherits the base OTs and extension model

nodes.subtitle: Improved Garbled Circuit: Free XOR Gates and Applications
nodes.summary: Free-XOR correlates the two labels on every wire through one global offset so XOR gates require neither garbled ciphertexts nor cryptographic operations, concentrating garbling cost on non-XOR gates.

metadata.title: A global wire-label offset makes XOR gates free in garbled circuits
metadata.statement: Free-XOR correlates the two labels on every wire through one global offset so XOR gates require neither garbled ciphertexts nor cryptographic operations, concentrating garbling cost on non-XOR gates.

historical_context.prior_boundary: Standard garbling treated XOR gates like other binary gates, assigning them ciphertext tables and cryptographic evaluation work even though XOR has linear structure.
historical_context.technical_delta: A shared global difference between zero and one wire labels lets the evaluator derive an XOR output label directly from the two input labels.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: It changed the practical cost model of garbled circuits and made XOR-rich circuit design a central optimization objective.
historical_context.narrative: Garbled-circuit cost had been accounted for gate by gate, with XOR operations consuming table entries and cryptographic calls alongside nonlinear gates. Free-XOR imposes one global offset between the two encodings of every wire. Under that invariant, XORing the evaluator's input labels already produces the correct output label, so the garbler sends no ciphertext for the gate. The atomic change is this wire-label invariant and the resulting zero garbling cost for XOR, under the paper's correlation-robustness assumptions. It mattered because the relevant concrete metric became the number of non-XOR gates, encouraging circuit representations and later garbling optimizations that preserve Free-XOR compatibility.

limitations: security requires the stated hash/correlation assumptions

sections.heading: Overview

sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes
sections.content: Locators refer to the ePrint PDF downloaded on 2026-10-11, which states no date. Printed page numbers run one behind PDF page numbers.

sections.heading: Main claims
sections.content: The setting is two parties, one statically corrupted by an active adversary, with security that includes complete fairness (§2.1, PDF p. 4). Theorem 3.2 (§3.2, PDF p. 16): assuming enhanced trapdoor permutations, every two-input function over polynomial-size domains without an embedded XOR, that is, without inputs \( x_0, x_1, y_0, y_1 \) such that \( f(x_i, y_j) = i \oplus j \), can be computed with complete fairness; the paper adds that oblivious transfer is both necessary and sufficient for this result. The proof reduces every such function to the greater-than function, Yao's millionaires' problem, whose protocol takes \( \Theta(m) \) rounds for domains of size m (§3, PDF p. 8), hence the restriction to polynomial-size domains; AND and OR are special cases. Section 4 shows that a particular function with an embedded XOR can be computed with complete fairness (Theorem 4.1, PDF p. 20), and Theorem 5.1 (§5, PDF p. 34) proves that every completely fair protocol for a function with an embedded XOR needs \( \omega(\log n) \) rounds in the security parameter n.

sections.heading: Open-question provenance
sections.content: Section 1.3 (PDF p. 3) calls a tight characterization of the Boolean functions that two parties can compute with complete fairness the most pressing question left open, notes that the positive results apply only to deterministic, single-output Boolean functions over polynomial-size domains, and asks about complete fairness for more parties without an honest majority. This supports characterizing fair two-party functions.

sections.heading: Historical role
sections.content: It opened the question of which two-party functions are fair, as MPC-PAPER-2014-ASHAROV and MPC-PAPER-2015-ABMO recall, and it settles the functions without an embedded XOR.

sections.heading: Limitations and unresolved review
sections.content: The positive results cover deterministic, single-output Boolean functions over polynomial-size domains (§1.3, PDF p. 3). The proofs were not audited.

metadata.title: End-to-end co-design makes semi-honest garbled-circuit 2PC practical
metadata.statement: Pinkas, Schneider, Smart, and Williams integrate circuit design, garbling, oblivious transfer, and systems optimizations into an end-to-end semi-honest two-party computation implementation evaluated on representative functions.

historical_context.prior_boundary: Garbled-circuit feasibility and isolated optimizations were known, but their combined end-to-end cost had not yet been demonstrated convincingly across a reusable implementation pipeline.
historical_context.technical_delta: The system coordinates circuit generation, Free-XOR-compatible garbling, OT handling, memory, and networking so the complete protocol rather than a single primitive is measured.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: It established implementation-aware co-design as a research contribution between abstract protocol construction and a versioned software artifact.
historical_context.narrative: By 2009, garbled circuits and oblivious transfer were established techniques, but practical claims could still be dominated by an unoptimized circuit, memory movement, public-key setup, or network handling. This work integrates those layers into one semi-honest two-party system and evaluates complete executions on representative functions. The atomic contribution is the end-to-end co-design showing how protocol and systems choices interact, not the invention of Yao garbling or Free-XOR. It mattered because MPC performance work gained a concrete whole-stack baseline and a systems methodology: optimize and account for the circuit, correlations, cryptographic kernels, and communication together rather than extrapolating practicality from one asymptotic component.

metadata.title: Boolean OR and three-party majority admit complete fairness without an honest majority
metadata.statement: Gordon and Katz construct completely fair protocols tolerating any t<n corruptions for n-party Boolean OR and three-party majority under suitable cryptographic assumptions, while proving that the latter requires super-logarithmic rounds.

historical_context.prior_boundary: Cleve's general impossibility and the immediately preceding two-party feasibility results left open whether any nontrivial multiparty functionality could achieve complete fairness without an honest majority.
historical_context.technical_delta: The paper gives an O(n)-round completely fair protocol for n-party Boolean OR and a super-logarithmic-round protocol for three-party majority, together with a round lower bound for the latter.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: It supplied the first positive multiparty examples in this regime and showed that feasibility and round complexity depend on the functionality rather than only the corruption threshold.
historical_context.narrative: Complete fairness was impossible for general dishonest-majority MPC, but earlier two-party results had already shown that this did not rule out every nontrivial function. Gordon and Katz carried that question into the multiparty setting. Under suitable cryptographic assumptions and a private broadcast channel or PKI, they give completely fair protocols for Boolean OR with any number of parties and for three-party majority while tolerating any t<n corruptions. The majority protocol requires super-logarithmic rounds, exposing a separation from its easier two-party partitions. The mapped boundary is therefore function-specific multiparty feasibility, not a generic upgrade from abort to fairness.

sections.heading: Main claims
sections.content: Theorem 1.1 (§1.1, PDF p. 3): assuming oblivious transfer, for every polynomial r there is an r-round two-party coin-flipping protocol that is \( 1/(4r-c) \)-secure for some constant c, so its bias is at most \( 1/(4r-c) \), while MPC-PAPER-1986-CLEVE shows bias at least \( 1/(8r+2) \). Here 1/p-security keeps the fully fair ideal model and lets the real and ideal executions be distinguished with probability at most 1/p plus a negligible term (§1, PDF pp. 2-3). A dealer, implemented by a protocol that is secure with abort, chooses a secret special round uniformly at random; before it the two parties' backup outputs are independent random bits, and from it on both equal the output (§3, PDF p. 10; Theorem 3.1, PDF p. 12). Section 4 refines the protocol to prove Theorem 1.1 and its extension to sampling from any polynomially-sampleable two-party distribution (Theorem 1.2, PDF p. 3; Theorem 4.1, PDF p. 17).

sections.heading: Open-question provenance
sections.content: The abstract and §1 (PDF pp. 1-2) state that whether the bound of MPC-PAPER-1986-CLEVE is tight had been open for over twenty years. Section 5 (PDF pp. 19-20) leaves open whether oblivious transfer is needed, how to close the factor-two gap to that bound, which the analysis of this protocol cannot close, and the optimal trade-off between the number of parties, the round complexity and the bias.

nodes.summary: TASTY provides a typed protocol-description language and runtime that generate and execute semi-honest two-party computations combining additively homomorphic encryption and garbled circuits, with explicit conversions between their value representations within one computation.

metadata.title: Typed HE and garbled values support mixed-protocol description and generation
metadata.statement: TASTY provides a typed protocol-description language and runtime that generate and execute semi-honest two-party computations combining additively homomorphic encryption and garbled circuits, with explicit conversions between their value representations within one computation.

historical_context.prior_boundary: Existing high-level SFE tools discussed by TASTY generally generated a single protocol family, while mixed HE/GC protocols and lower-level ways to describe cryptographic operations already existed.
historical_context.technical_delta: TASTYL exposes plain, homomorphic, and garbled value types and conversion operators in one protocol-description interface, from which the runtime generates and executes the specified mixed protocol.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The interface made mixed HE/GC protocols describable and executable without spelling out each underlying cryptographic message, while leaving representation choices visible to the programmer.
historical_context.narrative: Arithmetic and Boolean subcomputations can favor different secure-computation protocols, but using both requires explicit treatment of their intermediate values. Mixed HE/GC constructions already existed; TASTY brought them into a common protocol-description language and runtime. TASTYL distinguishes plain, homomorphic, and garbled values, and its typed operations and conversions describe how one computation crosses representation boundaries. The runtime generates and executes that description while abstracting away lower-level cryptographic messages. This supplied a practical mixed-protocol programming interface under a semi-honest two-party model. The programmer still specifies the representations: automatic selection between HE and garbled circuits is identified as future work, not as a capability established by this contribution.

source_locator.primary_source: IACR ePrint 2010/365 full version: §2 (model), PDF pp. 3–5; §2.3 and Figure 2, p. 5; §4–§4.1 and Figures 5–7, pp. 6–8; §6 (automatic-selection boundary), p. 12

qualifiers: Semi-honest two-party computation using the instantiated HE and garbled-circuit building blocks.
The program specifies typed representations and conversions; local inference of output types and bitlengths is not automatic protocol assignment.
The design separates input-independent setup from online work; this does not establish an unconditional reduction in total cost.
limitations: The underlying modular conversion framework and cryptographic primitives are prior building blocks, not separately claimed inventions of this atom.
Automatic compilation from a function-description language and automatic HE/GC selection are future work in §6.
No malicious or UC security guarantee, universal performance optimum, or portable benchmark ranking is admitted.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: TASTY typed mixed-protocol compiler The atomic object is the shared programming and execution interface for a programmer-specified mixture. In the example of §4.1.2 (Figures 6–7, PDF pages 7–8), products are computed homomorphically and the minimum is computed with garbled circuits after conversion. This supports direct mixed-domain membership; it does not make the card a new garbling construction or a new security-composition theorem. The source check covers the sections supporting this claim and its stated boundaries. It is not an independent proof verification or implementation reproduction.

sections.content: Locators refer to the ePrint full version, whose title page is dated 2012-10-04 and reads "Protocols for Multiparty Coin Toss With Dishonest Majority"; a footnote on PDF p. 1 refers to the CRYPTO 2010 paper as a preliminary version. Printed page numbers run one behind PDF page numbers. MPC-PAPER-2009-MNS (§1.3 of its 2015 revision) quotes the bias bound as in Theorem 4 below, while the abstract of MPC-PAPER-2016-AO and §1.3.1 of MPC-PAPER-2018-BHMO write it as \( O(2^{2^k}/r) \).

sections.heading: Main claims
sections.content: The parties communicate only over an authenticated broadcast channel in a synchronous network, against a static, computationally bounded, malicious and rushing adversary (§1.1, PDF pp. 4-5; §2, PDF p. 6); the results carry over to point-to-point channels with a public-key infrastructure at a multiplicative cost of O(m) rounds (PDF p. 5). A protocol has bias 1/p if it 1/p-securely computes coin tossing (Definition 2.5, PDF p. 8). Theorem 4 (§4, PDF p. 17): if enhanced trapdoor permutations exist, then for m parties and \( m/2 \le t < 2m/3 \) there is an r-round protocol tolerating t malicious parties with bias \( O(2^{2^{k+1}}/r') \), where \( k = 2t - m \) and \( r' = r - O(k+1) \). It combines a protocol with an on-line dealer (Theorem 5) with a secure implementation of the dealer (Theorem 6), and generalizes the special-round protocol of MPC-PAPER-2009-MNS. The bias is \( O(1/r) \) when m and t are constants (Corollary 2, §1.1, PDF p. 4) and when \( t = m/2 + O(1) \) (Corollary 3). For a constant fraction \( t = (1-\varepsilon)m \) of corrupted parties, Theorem 7 (§7, PDF p. 40) gives bias \( O(\varepsilon/\sqrt{r-t}) \), removing the factor t from the earlier \( O(t/\sqrt{r}) \) bound (§1.1, PDF p. 4).

sections.heading: Historical role
sections.content: It settles optimally fair coin flipping with fewer than two-thirds corrupted for a constant number of parties.

sections.heading: Limitations and unresolved review
sections.content: The bias grows doubly exponentially in the gap k between corrupted and honest parties, so it is \( O(1/r) \) only when that gap is constant; for two thirds or more corrupted parties the paper gives bias of order \( 1/\sqrt{r} \) (Theorem 7). The theorems assume enhanced trapdoor permutations; the paper states no version from oblivious transfer. The proofs were not audited.

historical_context.prior_boundary: Actively secure dishonest-majority arithmetic MPC carried expensive cryptographic checks through the live computation or relied on less efficient general compilers.
historical_context.technical_delta: SPDZ preprocesses authenticated multiplication correlations and attaches a global-MAC invariant to every shared value, leaving online arithmetic to local operations, openings, and batched verification.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: It established authenticated sharing as a durable active-security architecture whose online phase could survive repeated replacement of the offline generator.
historical_context.narrative: Dishonest-majority arithmetic MPC needed both multiplication resources and a way to detect parties that submitted inconsistent shares. SPDZ moves expensive somewhat-homomorphic computation into an input-independent preprocessing phase and equips each secret share with an information-theoretic MAC tied to a global hidden key. Online additions and triple-based multiplications remain simple, while batched checks detect forged openings. The atomic contribution is this authenticated-sharing architecture for active security, including its separation of offline correlation generation from online evaluation. It mattered because later systems could replace the original public-key-heavy preprocessing with OT-based or other generators while preserving the recognizable SPDZ online contract.

historical_context.prior_boundary: Practical malicious Boolean 2PC commonly strengthened passive protocols through generic compilation or replicated garbled circuits and cut-and-choose, both carrying substantial concrete overhead.
historical_context.technical_delta: TinyOT authenticates shared bits during OT-based preprocessing and evaluates Boolean circuits with cheap XORs, authenticated AND correlations, and batched checks tailored to the representation.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: It demonstrated that active security could be built into a Boolean-sharing architecture rather than added as a generic wrapper.
historical_context.narrative: Malicious two-party computation had often paid for security by compiling a passive protocol generically or checking many garbled circuits through cut-and-choose. TinyOT takes a representation-specific route. Its preprocessing uses oblivious transfer to create authenticated bits and related correlations; XOR remains local, while nonlinear operations and openings are protected by amortized consistency checks. The atomic contribution is the authenticated-bit architecture for active Boolean computation, not OT extension by itself and not a universal replacement for every garbling protocol. It mattered because it showed that specialized authentication could reduce the concrete cost of malicious security and created a Boolean counterpart to authenticated arithmetic-sharing designs.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Multiparty Computation with Low Communication, Computation and Interaction via Threshold FHE

sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes
sections.content: Locators refer to the ePrint PDF by Asharov, Jain and Wichs, whose title page is dated 2012-06-09. A version merged with work of López-Alt, Tromer and Vaikuntanathan appeared at EUROCRYPT 2012; that version was not checked here. Printed page numbers run one behind PDF page numbers.

sections.heading: Main claims
sections.content: With a common setup that can be a common random string, each party broadcasts a key share, and the sum of the shares is the public key of a threshold fully homomorphic encryption scheme based on LWE, of which each party holds a secret-key share (§1.1, PDF p. 4). Protocol 5.1 (§5, PDF p. 16) has three broadcast rounds: key generation; evaluation-key generation together with encryption of the inputs; and local homomorphic evaluation followed by joint decryption. Theorem 5.2 (§5, PDF p. 17): under LWE with suitable parameters, the protocol UC-realizes any deterministic polynomial-time function with a common output against a static semi-malicious adversary corrupting any number of the N parties; universally composable NIZKs in the common-random-string model give security against malicious adversaries without extra rounds (§6, PDF p. 17; Theorem E.3, PDF p. 36). Treating the first-round message as a public key gives two rounds with a reusable public-key infrastructure (§1.2, PDF p. 5; §6, PDF p. 18). With the leveled scheme, communication is proportional to the number of multiplicative levels of the circuit; bootstrapping makes key generation and decryption independent of circuit size, at the price of a non-standard circular-security assumption for the basic LWE-based scheme (§6, PDF pp. 18-19). The only computation that depends on the circuit is the homomorphic evaluation, which a single party or an external server can perform (§1.2, PDF p. 5; §6, PDF p. 19).

sections.heading: Historical role
sections.content: It settles communication independent of circuit size from LWE and circular security, the computational counterpart of the circuit-size question.

sections.heading: Limitations and unresolved review
sections.content: Security is computational and uses a common random string or public-key setup whose size grows with the number of parties (footnotes 3 and 4, PDF p. 5). Communication independent of circuit size needs the circular-security assumption; under LWE alone it grows with the circuit's multiplicative depth. The proofs were not audited.

metadata.title: On the Power of Correlated Randomness in Secure Computation
versions: author draft of the TCC 2013 paper (20 PDF pages; no ePrint ID)
metadata.review_scope: Author draft of the TCC 2013 paper, PDF downloaded 2026-10-11: abstract and §1 (PDF pp. 1-6), §2 (PDF pp. 7-9), §3 with Theorems 1-3, Figure 2 and Claim 1 (PDF pp. 9-12), Theorem 4 (§4.1, PDF p. 14) and Theorem 14 (Appendix B, PDF p. 20), read for the communication question in the correlated-randomness model and its answer with exponential correlated randomness; page numbers differ from LNCS 7785; proofs deferred to the full version not reviewed; no separate contribution record.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: On the Power of Correlated Randomness in Secure Computation

sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes
sections.content: Locators refer to an author draft of the TCC 2013 paper whose title and authors match the LNCS version. It has no ePrint ID and no printed page numbers, so locators give PDF pages, which differ from LNCS 7785 pp. 600-620. The draft defers several proofs, the n-party generalization of its protocols, and Theorems 9-15 (stated in Appendix B) to a full version that was not read.

sections.heading: Main claims
sections.content: The paper studies two-party computation and multiparty computation without an honest majority, where before the inputs are known the parties receive correlated random strings from a fixed joint distribution (§1, PDF p. 2; §2, PDF p. 8). Its positive results hold for UC security with adaptive corruptions (§2, PDF p. 8). Earlier protocols in this model communicate in proportion to circuit size (§1, PDF p. 3). Theorem 1 (§3.1, PDF p. 9): every n-party functionality has a two-round protocol with perfect security against semi-honest parties, total communication \( O(\alpha) \) and storage, the number of correlated random bits the parties receive, \( O(\alpha 2^\alpha) \), where \( \alpha \) is the total input length. The two-party protocol uses one-time truth tables, additive shares of a truth table whose rows and columns are shifted by random offsets, each offset known to one party (Figure 2 and Claim 1, PDF p. 10). Theorem 2 (PDF p. 9) gives statistical security with abort against malicious parties, given broadcast, with communication \( O(\alpha + n \log(1/\varepsilon)) \); Theorem 3 gives perfect security against malicious parties for two-party sender-receiver functionalities, where only one party receives output. Theorem 4 (§4.1, PDF p. 14): XOR with output to both parties has no perfectly secure protocol with abort in this model. Section 1 (PDF pp. 3-4) gives evidence that the exponential storage is inherent, through Theorem 14 (Appendix B, PDF p. 20, stated without proof): if every sender-receiver functionality on n-bit inputs had a semi-honest statistically secure protocol with r(n) bits of correlated randomness and c(n) bits of communication, there would be a three-server statistical private information retrieval protocol with communication \( O(r(\log N) + c(\log N) + \log N) \) for databases of size N. Section 1 notes that polynomial storage for every two-party functionality would thus give an unexpected answer to a long-standing open question on information-theoretic private information retrieval.

sections.heading: Open-question provenance
sections.content: The abstract and Question 1 of §1 (PDF pp. 1-3) record that earlier protocols left open whether, with correlated randomness, the communication of unconditionally secure computation can be made independent of the circuit size, for two parties and for many parties without an honest majority. This supports sublinear communication with trusted correlated randomness. Theorem 1 answers the question with correlated randomness exponential in the input length, settling the case of exponential correlated randomness.

sections.heading: Limitations and unresolved review
sections.content: The communication-optimal protocols need correlated randomness exponential in the input length, and the evidence that this is inherent rests on Theorem 14, which the draft states without proof. Proofs deferred to the full version were not reviewed.

nodes.title: Conversion-aware cost models drive automatic HE and garbled-circuit assignment
nodes.subtitle: Automatic Protocol Selection in Secure Two-Party Computations
nodes.summary: For a specified single-static-assignment intermediate program and forecast cost model, Kerschbaum, Schneider, and Schröpfer formulate assignment of operations to HE-assisted arithmetic sharing or garbled circuits with conversion costs, and give a 0–1 integer-programming formulation and a cost-decreasing greedy heuristic for choosing the mixed protocol.

metadata.title: Conversion-aware cost models drive automatic HE and garbled-circuit assignment
metadata.statement: For a specified single-static-assignment intermediate program and forecast cost model, Kerschbaum, Schneider, and Schröpfer formulate assignment of operations to HE-assisted arithmetic sharing or garbled circuits with conversion costs, and give a 0–1 integer-programming formulation and a cost-decreasing greedy heuristic for choosing the mixed protocol.

historical_context.prior_boundary: Mixed-protocol systems such as TASTY exposed representation choices, but the programmer still selected which subcomputations used each protocol; choosing operations independently could overlook conversion costs.
historical_context.technical_delta: The assignment objective combines operation forecasts with costs for converting each reused intermediate value at most once, and is addressed by integer programming and a greedy protocol-selection algorithm.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: Protocol selection became an explicit optimization problem over the intermediate program and deployment cost parameters rather than only a manual decomposition of the function.
historical_context.narrative: Mixed-protocol interfaces already allowed arithmetic and Boolean subcomputations to use different representations, but the programmer had to choose the partition. Kerschbaum, Schneider, and Schröpfer make that choice an explicit cost-model problem. Their intermediate program exposes operation dependencies, while the objective accounts for both protocol execution and conversions, reusing a converted value across its consumers. An integer-programming formulation and a cost-decreasing greedy heuristic address the same assignment problem. The resulting contribution is automatic, conversion-aware selection between the instantiated HE-assisted sharing and garbled-circuit protocols. Its optimality target is the forecast objective, not universal wall-clock performance; the source also leaves hardness of the specific partitioning problem as a conjecture.

source_locator.primary_source: IACR ePrint 2014/200 full version: §3.2–§3.4, PDF pp. 3–4; §4–§4.2, pp. 4–5; §5 and Definition 1, pp. 5–6; §5.1–§5.2 and Algorithm 1, pp. 6–7; §6 and Tables 1–2 for forecast-only evaluation context

qualifiers: Semi-honest two-party setting; the instantiated arithmetic protocol maintains additive shares modulo 2^l and uses Paillier-assisted operations.

Assignment is over the supported three-operand single-static-assignment intermediate language, with program bitlengths, security parameters, local operation costs, and network parameters supplied to the forecast model.
Conversion between the HE-assisted share representation and garbled values is charged at most once per intermediate value and reused by its consumers.
The instantiated security assumptions and cited composition argument are those in §3; protocol selection itself supplies no stronger adversary guarantee.
limitations: Integer-programming optimality is relative to the modeled objective; the source discusses approximation of execution costs, including neighboring-operation effects.
The greedy method starts with garbled-circuit assignments and accepts cost-decreasing changes to HE; no general approximation ratio is admitted.
Section 5 conjectures NP-hardness of the specific partitioning problem and explicitly does not prove it.
The use-case comparisons are forecast results in specified settings, not universal measured speedups or cross-system rankings.
This atom is not a general automatic compiler for all MPC representations, a new malicious or UC security theorem, or a separate garbling construction.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Conversion-aware automatic protocol selection The HE label in the selection problem refers to the HE-assisted computation on additive shares described in §3.2, not to the direct ciphertext value representation used by TASTY. Section 3.3 converts those shares into garbled inputs, or garbled outputs into shares, using circuits over their bitlength. Section 4.2 incorporates the conversion boundary into the assignment cost. These details support the one assignment claim; they do not automatically create distinct sharing, garbling, or security-foundation contributions. The source check covers the sections supporting this claim and its stated boundaries. It is not an independent proof verification, solver audit, or implementation reproduction.

metadata.title: Towards Characterizing Complete Fairness in Secure Two-Party Computation
metadata.review_scope: ePrint 2014/098 full version dated 2014-02-10: abstract and §1-§1.2 (PDF pp. 1-8), §2.1.1 (PDF p. 9), §4.3 with Theorem 4.13 (PDF pp. 26-27) and §5 with Theorem 5.1 and Corollaries 5.2, 5.5 and 5.6 (PDF pp. 28-34), read for the characterization question and the classes shown fair; proofs not audited; no separate contribution record.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Towards Characterizing Complete Fairness in Secure Two-Party Computation

sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes
sections.content: Locators refer to the ePrint full version, whose title page is dated 2014-02-10. PDF page numbers run one ahead of the printed page numbers.

sections.heading: Main claims
sections.content: The setting is two parties, one statically and maliciously corrupted, with full security including complete fairness (§2.1.1, PDF p. 9). Theorem 1.1 (§1.2, PDF p. 7): assuming oblivious transfer, a Boolean function whose rows, as points in \( \mathbb{R}^m \), have a full-dimensional convex hull can be computed with complete fairness, using the protocol of MPC-PAPER-2008-GHKL and tools from convex geometry. Almost all Boolean functions whose two domains differ in size have this property (§1.1, PDF p. 4). Functions that are not full-dimensional and meet further conditions, almost always met when the domains have equal size, cannot be computed by the protocol of MPC-PAPER-2008-GHKL with its simulation strategy (§1.1, PDF p. 5). Theorem 4.13 (§4.3, PDF p. 27) combines these results with the known criterion for functions that imply fair coin tossing and leaves one subclass of symmetric Boolean functions not characterized. Theorem 1.2 (§1.2, PDF p. 7) extends the protocol to a large class of asymmetric Boolean functions, including every function whose second party's output is full-dimensional (Corollary 5.2, PDF p. 30), and, for every finite range \( \Sigma \), to a class of functions with non-binary output; the criterion for non-binary output can hold only when \( |X| > (|\Sigma| - 1) \cdot |Y| \).

sections.heading: Open-question provenance
sections.content: The abstract (PDF p. 1) and §1 (PDF p. 3) call which functions can be computed with complete fairness the fundamental question raised by MPC-PAPER-2008-GHKL, and §1 (PDF p. 4) asks whether fairness is possible over larger ranges or for asymmetric functions. The "Open problems" paragraph of §1.2 (PDF p. 8) presents the paper as a step towards a full characterization of fairness for finite-domain functions and names finalizing it the main open question; it also asks about infinite domains and, for non-binary outputs, other ratios of domain sizes. Section 1.1 (PDF p. 5) leaves open the functions to which neither the protocol of MPC-PAPER-2008-GHKL nor the coin-tossing impossibility applies. These support characterizing fair two-party functions.

sections.heading: Limitations and unresolved review
sections.content: The subclass of symmetric Boolean functions left open in Theorem 4.13 was later settled by MPC-PAPER-2015-ABMO. The negative result rules out only the protocol of MPC-PAPER-2008-GHKL with its simulation strategy, not every protocol (§1.1, PDF p. 5). The proofs were not audited.

sections.heading: Main claims
sections.content: Theorem 1.1 (§1.1): assuming oblivious transfer, for every r there is an r-round three-party coin-flipping protocol with bias \( O(\log^3 r/r) \) against one or two corrupted parties. Before it, the best protocol for two thirds or more corrupted parties, including the three-party case, had bias about \( t/\sqrt{r} \) for t corrupted parties. The protocol is a variant of the majority protocol rather than of the threshold-round approach of MPC-PAPER-2009-MNS and MPC-PAPER-2010-BOO. Section 1 notes that the \( \Omega(1/r) \) lower bound of MPC-PAPER-1986-CLEVE extends to many parties by a simple reduction.

sections.heading: Open-question provenance
sections.content: Section 1.4 leaves open whether an optimally fair three-party protocol exists, without the polylogarithmic factor, and whether fair coin flipping is possible for more than three parties against any number of corruptions. These support optimally fair coin flipping for three or more parties and the three-party case; the theorem settles three-party coin flipping within a polylogarithmic factor.

historical_context.narrative: Distributed BMR garbling promised online rounds independent of circuit depth, but maliciously secure preparation of the garbled circuit remained a concrete obstacle. This work uses the arithmetic engine during preprocessing to construct and check the BMR garbling, after which the parties enter a two-round online phase and evaluate locally. The atomic contribution is this division of labor between authenticated arithmetic preparation and garbled Boolean evaluation. It mattered because it showed that a useful protocol stack need not belong to one mechanism family: components could be composed across domains while preserving an explicit malicious dishonest-majority contract.

metadata.statement: Half-gates decomposes a garbled AND into evaluator and garbler halves, reaching two ciphertexts per AND gate while remaining compatible with the Free-XOR wire-label invariant.

historical_context.prior_boundary: Free-XOR removed the cost of linear gates, leaving garbled non-XOR gates as the dominant communication term and prior compatible techniques above the two-ciphertext target.
historical_context.technical_delta: The construction splits the AND function into two correlated half-gates whose outputs combine under the global offset, requiring one ciphertext for each half.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: It established a new concrete communication point for standard Free-XOR-compatible garbling and sharpened the non-XOR gate cost metric.
historical_context.narrative: Once Free-XOR made linear gates costless, the bandwidth of a garbled circuit was governed primarily by its AND gates. Existing Free-XOR-compatible garbling still sent more material per nonlinear gate. Half-gates decomposes each AND into a garbler half and an evaluator half, arranging the label algebra so that each half needs one ciphertext and their outputs recombine correctly. The atomic contribution is the two-ciphertext AND construction under the compatible garbling model, not a claim about total protocol latency. It mattered because it set a widely used concrete cost point for garbled-circuit implementations and made AND count an even cleaner predictor of communication.

metadata.title: Complete Characterization of Fairness in Secure Two-Party Computation of Boolean Functions
metadata.review_scope: ePrint 2014/1000 PDF dated 2014-12-16: abstract and §1-§1.2 (PDF pp. 1-4), §2.1 (PDF pp. 5-7), §3 with Remark 3.1, Theorem 3.3, Corollary 3.6 and Theorems 3.9, 3.11 and 3.12 (PDF pp. 7-16), §4 with Theorems 4.1, 4.4 and 4.6 (PDF pp. 17-23), §5 through Theorem 5.6 (PDF pp. 27-30) and §6 (PDF p. 35), read for the two-party characterization, the asymmetric gap and the multiparty corruption threshold; proofs not audited; no separate contribution record.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Complete Characterization of Fairness in Secure Two-Party Computation of Boolean Functions

sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes
sections.content: Locators refer to the ePrint PDF, whose title page is dated 2014-12-16. Printed page numbers run one behind PDF page numbers.

sections.heading: Main claims
sections.content: Security is full security, including complete fairness, against a non-uniform polynomial-time malicious adversary (§2.1, Definition 2.3, PDF p. 7). Protocols are described with an on-line dealer, which a secure-with-abort protocol for oblivious transfer removes (Remark 3.1, PDF p. 7). Theorem 3.9 (§3.2, PDF p. 14): assuming oblivious transfer, a Boolean two-party function with a common output and matrix M can be computed with full security if and only if it is not semi-balanced, if and only if the all-zero or the all-one vector is an affine combination of the rows or of the columns of M. Possibility uses a variant of the protocol of MPC-PAPER-2008-GHKL (Theorem 3.3 and Corollary 3.6, PDF pp. 8-12); impossibility for semi-balanced functions rests on an earlier reduction to fair sampling (proof of Theorem 3.9). Theorem 3.12 (PDF p. 16) extends the characterization to randomized Boolean functions. For asymmetric Boolean functions, Theorem 4.1 (§4.1, PDF p. 17) gives a sufficient condition that generalizes Theorem 3.3, and Theorem 4.4 (§4.2, PDF p. 20) a necessary condition that generalizes the semi-balanced criterion. A protocol in which the input of the first party decides which party learns the output first shows one function in the gap to be fair (Theorem 4.6, §4.3, PDF p. 23; §6, PDF p. 35). For more parties, Theorem 5.1 (§5, PDF p. 27): for a constant even number \( m = 2k \) of parties and an adversary corrupting up to k of them, a deterministic function, or a randomized Boolean function, with a common output can be computed with full security if and only if every split of the parties into two sets of size k yields a two-party function computable with full security. With §3 this characterizes the Boolean functions computable with fairness when the number of parties is constant and at most half of them can be malicious (abstract, PDF p. 1; §1.2, PDF p. 4).

sections.heading: Open-question provenance
sections.content: The abstract (PDF p. 1), §1.2 (PDF p. 4) and the opening of §4 (PDF p. 17) state that a gap is left between the sufficient and the necessary condition for asymmetric Boolean functions and that the classification of the functions in the gap remains open. Section 6 (PDF p. 35) asks which asymmetric functions can be computed when a protocol may split the parties' inputs arbitrarily, gives a function in the gap whose fairness its methods do not settle, and calls the characterization for arbitrary output domains a hard problem; it also asks about multiparty Boolean functions with a strict majority corrupted and about input domains that grow with the security parameter. These support the asymmetric Boolean case and characterizing fair two-party functions.

sections.heading: Historical role
sections.content: It settles fairness for symmetric Boolean functions, answering the open problem of MPC-PAPER-2008-GHKL for that class (§1.2, PDF p. 3), and names the asymmetric Boolean case open.

sections.heading: Limitations and unresolved review
sections.content: The protocols assume input domains of constant size; §6 (PDF p. 35) notes that domains of size logarithmic in the security parameter keep rounds and computation polynomial. Section 5 treats only common outputs and only the threshold \( t = m/2 \) with m even. The proofs were not audited.

metadata.title: OT-based checks replace public-key-heavy SPDZ triple generation
metadata.statement: MASCOT generates actively secure authenticated arithmetic triples from oblivious transfer, multiplication, and consistency checks, replacing SPDZ's somewhat-homomorphic-encryption preprocessing while preserving its online sharing protocol.

historical_context.prior_boundary: The original SPDZ architecture had a light online phase but generated authenticated multiplication triples through expensive somewhat-homomorphic encryption.
historical_context.technical_delta: MASCOT derives candidate products from OT, authenticates them, and applies sacrifice and consistency checks to obtain maliciously secure triples without the original homomorphic-encryption generator.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: It showed that an MPC online architecture could remain stable while its correlation backend was independently replaced for better concrete performance.
historical_context.narrative: SPDZ had already isolated its expensive work in preprocessing, but the original somewhat-homomorphic-encryption machinery made that phase costly. MASCOT keeps the authenticated arithmetic shares and online protocol intact while replacing the triple generator. Oblivious-transfer-based multiplication creates candidate correlations, and authentication plus sacrifice-style checks remove malformed values under malicious behavior. The atomic contribution is this OT-based preprocessing replacement, not a new online arithmetic semantics. It mattered because it validated the modular promise of the SPDZ architecture: researchers and systems could optimize correlation generation as an independent technical thread while retaining the same actively secure dishonest-majority online interface.

source_locator.primary_source: ePrint 2016/505 (PDF generated 2016-09-14), §1.1 (pp. 3–4), §1.2 (pp. 4–5), §2 and §2.1 (pp. 7–8), §3 Protocol 1 and Theorem 1 (pp. 8–10), §4 and Theorem 2 (pp. 10–16), §5 Protocol 4, Theorem 3 and Corollary 1 (pp. 16–19), §6 Theorems 4–5 and Protocol 6 (pp. 19–21), §7.1 Table 2 (pp. 22–23); PDF page numbers match printed pages

qualifiers: Arithmetic triples over F_p or F_2^k; Theorem 3 uses τ = 4 combined triples for statistical security k, and Corollary 1 allows τ = 3 at k/2 (p. 19).
Malicious, static corruption of up to n − 1 parties, proved in the UC framework (§2, p. 7).
The OT instances are assumed secure against malicious parties (footnote 2, p. 4); base OTs are a one-time setup excluded from the complexity count (§7.1, p. 22).
The online phase is essentially that of SPDZ with Beaver multiplication (§6.2, Theorem 5, pp. 20–21).
limitations: Preprocessing and checks remain nontrivial; triple communication is n(n − 1)(τλk + (τ + 5)k²) bits (§7.1, p. 22).
Performance figures depend on the OT-extension implementation and network context; Table 1 compares against earlier SPDZ implementations, not a context-independent baseline.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: MASCOT triples The optimization is attached to the SPDZ preprocessing boundary rather than classified as an implementation. The full text names three mapped predecessors. Correlated oblivious product evaluation is built from the IKNP OT extension (§2, p. 7; §3, p. 8). The online phase is SPDZ's (§1.1, p. 4; §6.2, p. 20). Multiplication uses Beaver's circuit randomization (§5, p. 16; §6.2, p. 20). TinyOT appears only in related work, as one of several protocols that use OT extension for binary circuits (§1.3, p. 6).

metadata.review_scope: ePrint 2016/800 PDF downloaded 2026-10-11: abstract and §1-§1.3.4 (PDF pp. 1-10), §2.2 (PDF pp. 14-15), Theorem 9, Corollary 1 and Lemma 6 (§3.3, PDF p. 27) and the proof sketch of Corollary 1 (§3.3.1, PDF p. 30), read for the bias bound, corruption threshold, assumption and communication model; proofs not audited; no separate contribution record.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Almost-Optimally Fair Multiparty Coin-Tossing with Nearly Three-Quarters Malicious

sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes
sections.content: Locators refer to the ePrint PDF downloaded on 2026-10-11, which states no date; a footnote on PDF p. 1 refers to the TCC 2016-B paper as a preliminary version. Printed page numbers equal PDF page numbers. MPC-PAPER-2018-BHMO (§1.3.1) states the bias as \( \tilde O(2^{2^m}/r) \), which agrees with Corollary 1 below.

sections.heading: Main claims
sections.content: The parties communicate only over a synchronous broadcast channel, against a static, computationally bounded, malicious and rushing adversary; most of the analysis is for fail-stop adversaries, and standard techniques then give a protocol against malicious adversaries with the same bias and round complexity (§2.2, PDF pp. 14-15). Corollary 1 (§3.3, PDF p. 27): assuming oblivious transfer, for constants m and \( t < 3m/4 \) and every polynomial r, there is an r-round m-party coin-tossing protocol with bias \( O(2^{2^m}\log^3 r/r) \) against every efficient adversary corrupting up to t parties; Theorem 1 (§1.1, PDF p. 3) states it informally. The protocol uses the secret-sharing technique of MPC-PAPER-2010-BOO to reduce the problem to the constructions of MPC-PAPER-2014-HT: applied to the derandomized two-party protocol of MPC-PAPER-2014-HT it gives an auxiliary protocol for fewer than two thirds corrupted, which then supplies the defense values of the final protocol (§1.3.4, PDF p. 8). The factor \( 2^{2^m} \) arises because in each round the adversary sees defense values for many corrupted subsets, which is why m must be constant (§1.1, PDF p. 3).

sections.heading: Historical role
sections.content: It settles coin flipping within a polylogarithmic factor with fewer than three quarters corrupted.

sections.heading: Limitations and unresolved review
sections.content: The bound holds only for a constant number of parties. The passage from fail-stop to malicious adversaries is given as a proof sketch (§3.3.1, PDF p. 30). The proofs were not audited.
