nodes.summary: On the Communication Required for Unconditionally Secure Multiplication

metadata.title: On the Communication Required for Unconditionally Secure Multiplication
metadata.review_scope: ePrint 2015/1097 PDF downloaded 2026-10-11: abstract and §1-§1.1 (PDF pp. 1-6), §2 model (PDF p. 7), Definition 7, Theorem 1 and Corollary 1 (§3, PDF pp. 11-13), Theorems 2-3 (PDF pp. 16-18), Theorems 4 and 7 (§4, PDF pp. 20 and 26) and §5 Conclusions (PDF p. 28), read for the open question on communication below circuit size and the scope of the gate-by-gate lower bounds; proofs not audited; no separate contribution record.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: On the Communication Required for Unconditionally Secure Multiplication

sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes
sections.content: Locators refer to the ePrint PDF downloaded on 2026-10-11. The PDF states no revision date; its file date, 2016-06-07, matches the latest ePrint revision. It has no printed page numbers, so locators give PDF pages.

sections.heading: Main claims
sections.content: The model is synchronous protocols over point-to-point secure channels, with static passive corruption of t of the n players, statistical security, and no bound on computation; communication patterns may be dynamic (§1.1, PDF p. 3; §2, PDF p. 7). A gate-by-gate protocol calls, for every multiplication gate, a multiplication gate protocol that turns random shares of a and b into random shares of ab (Definition 7, PDF p. 11). Theorem 1 (§3, PDF p. 12): with an honest majority, every such protocol has expected anticipated message complexity above 2t. By Corollary 1 (PDF p. 13), a gate-by-gate protocol secure against \( t = \Theta(n) \) corruptions communicates \( \Omega(n \cdot |C|) \) bits, and an ordered one needs a number of rounds proportional to the multiplicative depth of C. No such bound on a single multiplication gate protocol can grow with the field size (§3, PDF p. 14). For k parallel multiplications, the players in any set of n − 2t players together perform \( \Omega(k) \) multiplications (Theorem 2, PDF p. 16), and regular protocols with ideal sharing, such as Shamir's, communicate \( \Omega(k) \) (Theorem 3, PDF p. 18). With preprocessing and n − 1 passive corruptions, every multiplication gate protocol with additive output sharing has expected anticipated message complexity above n − 1 (Theorem 4, §4.1, PDF p. 20). For an arbitrary output sharing scheme, a protocol producing shares of f(a, b) needs more than t messages once secure computation of f needs more preprocessed data than reconstruction of that sharing consumes (Theorem 7, §4.2, PDF p. 26). The abstract states that known gate-by-gate protocols meet these bounds up to constant factors.

sections.heading: Open-question provenance
sections.content: The abstract (PDF p. 1) calls whether information-theoretic protocols inherently need more communication and rounds than computationally secure ones open and probably very hard. Section 1 (PDF p. 2) calls communication much smaller than the circuit size, for protocols that stay polynomial in the circuit size, a long-standing open problem, and notes that computational assumptions make it possible. Section 5 (PDF p. 28) names whether the bounds hold for every protocol efficient in the circuit size the main problem the paper leaves open. These support information-theoretic MPC with communication sublinear in circuit size, for which the paper supplies the main known obstacle.

sections.heading: Limitations and unresolved review
sections.content: The lower bounds apply only to gate-by-gate protocols, not to every information-theoretic protocol, and they do not count the communication for sharing inputs or reconstructing outputs (§1.1, PDF p. 6). The dishonest-majority bound of Theorem 4 assumes additive output sharing. The proofs were not audited.

sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes
sections.content: The reviewed copy is the ePrint 2016/505 PDF generated on 2016-09-14. Its PDF page numbers match the printed pages. The CCS 2016 proceedings version was not compared.

sections.heading: Atomic contribution
sections.content: MPC-CONTRIB-2016-MASCOT-TRIPLES records the OT-based authenticated-triple generator. The checked locators are §1.1–§1.2 (pp. 3–5), the UC model with static corruption of up to n − 1 parties in §2 (p. 7), COPE in §3 (Protocol 1, Theorem 1, pp. 8–10), authentication in §4 (Theorem 2, p. 16), triple generation in §5 (Protocol 4, Theorem 3, Corollary 1, pp. 17–19), the preprocessing and online protocols in §6 (Theorems 4–5, pp. 19–21), and the complexity count in §7.1 (pp. 22–23).

sections.heading: Relations
sections.content: IKNP OT extension [25]: the OT-extension form MASCOT uses (§2, p. 7) and the base of COPE (§3, p. 8). SPDZ [18]: the online phase is identical to SPDZ's (§1.1, p. 4; §6.2, p. 20), and the sacrifice step follows [16, 18] (§5, p. 18). Beaver's circuit randomization [4]: used for online multiplication (§5, p. 16; §6.2, p. 20). TinyOT [10, 32, 36] and GMW [2, 22] appear only in related work, as protocols that use OT extension for binary circuits (§1.3, p. 6). No dependency on them is recorded. MASCOT generalizes the binary-field OT triple generation of Frederiksen et al. [20] to large fields (§1.1, p. 3). It starts from Gilboa's product sharing [21] (§1.2, p. 4), and its implementation optimizes the actively secure OT extension of Keller et al. [28] (§7.2, p. 22). None of these has a card. The implementation reference [29] is the SPDZ-2 repository. The paper does not name MP-SPDZ, so the MASCOT-to-MP-SPDZ relation still rests on MP-SPDZ's own sources.

sections.heading: Limitations and unresolved review
sections.content: This review checks statements, models, and locators, not an independent verification of the security proofs or the reported measurements.

metadata.title: Single-execution malicious garbled 2PC reduces setup and circuit-processing cost
metadata.statement: Wang, Malozemoff, and Katz optimize malicious garbled-circuit two-party computation for a single execution by reducing public-key work and improving oblivious-transfer and circuit-processing bottlenecks, with an open implementation supporting the evaluation.

historical_context.prior_boundary: Malicious 2PC protocols often amortized setup across repeated executions or paid substantial public-key and checking costs when evaluated as a single run.
historical_context.technical_delta: The protocol and implementation co-optimize base cryptography, OT handling, and garbled-circuit processing for the one-execution regime rather than assuming a long amortization horizon.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: It made the amortization unit explicit and supplied a concrete systems-security transition without confusing the protocol optimization with the released software version.
historical_context.narrative: Practical malicious two-party computation was frequently evaluated under amortization assumptions that spread setup and public-key operations across many executions. That model can hide the cost faced by an application that invokes the protocol only once. Wang, Malozemoff, and Katz redesign and implement the malicious garbled-circuit path around this single-execution boundary, reducing public-key work and streamlining OT and circuit processing. The atomic contribution is the implementation-aware protocol optimization for that amortization unit; the EMP codebase is a related artifact with its own identity. It mattered because later comparisons had to state whether costs were per run or amortized rather than treating all practical 2PC results as directly comparable.

sections.heading: Overview

sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes
sections.content: The ECCC report states that the survey appears in a volume in honor of Oded Goldreich's 60th birthday (Tutorials on the Foundations of Cryptography). Locators refer to the ECCC version.

sections.heading: Main claims
sections.content: Theorem 3.4 (p. 10) gives perfect decomposable affine encodings for arithmetic circuits of logarithmic depth, and Theorem 4.1 (p. 17) perfect encodings of degree three and locality four for arithmetic branching programs. Theorem 4.2 (p. 18) encodes all polynomial-size circuits in degree three, but with computational privacy from one-way functions computable in NC¹. Section 5.1 (p. 29) explains that securely computing a function reduces to computing its encoding, that encodings of constant degree can be computed in a constant number of rounds, and that this gives constant-round information-theoretic protocols for log-space functions.

sections.heading: Open-question provenance
sections.content: Section 3.2 (p. 10) calls efficient perfect or statistical encodings for general polynomial-size circuits, or even for circuits of depth \( \log^2 n \), wide open, and §6 (p. 31) asks again for efficiently computable perfectly secure encodings of polynomial-size circuits, also for constant degree. This is the route constant-degree statistical encodings for all circuits to constant-round information-theoretic MPC.

sections.heading: Limitations and unresolved review
sections.content: It is a survey and proves no new result on information-theoretic encodings; its open questions reflect the literature up to 2017.

sections.heading: Main claims
sections.content: Theorem 1.1 (§1.1): assuming oblivious transfer, for t parties with \( t \le \frac12 \log\log r \) there is an r-round coin-flipping protocol tolerating up to t − 1 corrupted parties with bias \( O\bigl(t^4 2^t \sqrt{\log r} / r^{1/2 + 1/(2^{t-1}-2)}\bigr) \), so \( r^{-1/2-\Theta(1)} \) for a constant number of parties. The remark after the theorem gives a three-party protocol with bias \( O(\sqrt{\log r}/r) \), improving MPC-PAPER-2014-HT.

sections.heading: Open-question provenance
sections.content: Section 1.5 calls finding the optimal bias of t-party coin flipping for \( t > 2 \) the main open question of the area, notes that for more than three parties the gap between upper and lower bounds is still large, and leaves open whether the remaining \( \sqrt{\log r} \) factor is needed for three parties. This supports optimally fair coin flipping for three or more parties; Theorem 1.1 settles coin flipping with polynomially larger bias for every constant number of parties.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Designing Fully Secure Protocols for Secure Two-Party Computation of Constant-Domain Functions

sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes
sections.content: Locators refer to the ePrint PDF downloaded on 2026-10-11, which states no date; proofs of some results follow the paper as supplementary material (§1.2, PDF p. 4). Printed page numbers equal PDF page numbers.

sections.heading: Main claims
sections.content: The setting is two parties, one corrupted by a computationally bounded malicious adversary, with full security (§2.1, PDF pp. 5-6). Protocols are described in the online dealer model, which a standard transformation turns into plain-model protocols (PDF p. 7). Section 3 introduces security against sampling attacks, a necessary condition for fair protocols. Theorem 4.1 (§4.1, PDF p. 16): a protocol that is constant-round, passively secure and secure against sampling attacks can be turned into a fully secure protocol for the same function, by adding a threshold round in the spirit of MPC-PAPER-2008-GHKL. The construction applies to every constant-domain two-party function, including randomized, asymmetric and non-Boolean ones (§1.2, PDF p. 4). Section 5 gives an algorithm that takes an asymmetric Boolean function and either returns such a protocol or fails; §5.3 (PDF p. 30) uses it to prove fair an asymmetric function that MPC-PAPER-2015-ABMO posed as an open problem. Section 3 (PDF p. 7) describes the semi-balanced criterion of MPC-PAPER-2015-ABMO and related work as the only known necessary condition for fairness.

sections.heading: Open-question provenance
sections.content: Section 1 (PDF p. 2) takes as its subject the characterization of functions with respect to fairness, the fundamental question raised by MPC-PAPER-2008-GHKL, and §1.1 defines it as finding a necessary and sufficient condition for a two-party function to be fair. The abstract states that the characterization remains open, and §1.2 (PDF p. 4) that the paper's methods do not settle it for constant-domain functions, even for asymmetric Boolean functions. Section 6 (PDF p. 32) adds that the algorithm fails on some functions that are not semi-balanced, whose status is unknown, and conjectures that such a failure essentially indicates impossibility. These support characterizing fair two-party functions and the asymmetric Boolean case.

sections.heading: Limitations and unresolved review
sections.content: That the algorithm fails only on functions that cannot be computed fairly is a conjecture (§6, PDF p. 32). The paper says little about multiparty settings with a dishonest majority or about functions that depend on the security parameter (§6, PDF p. 33). The proofs were not audited.

metadata.title: Pseudorandom correlation generators move large OT batches to local seed expansion
metadata.statement: Boyle, Couteau, Gilboa, Ishai, Kohl, and Scholl formalize pseudorandom correlation generators and construct silent OT-style expansion, replacing communication and stored correlated randomness with short seeds and local computation.

historical_context.prior_boundary: OT extension made each additional transfer cheap in public-key terms, but producing very large correlation batches still required communication and storage proportional to the batch.
historical_context.technical_delta: A PCG lets parties expand compact correlated seeds locally into a much larger structured correlation, including silent OT constructions under the paper's assumptions.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: It made communication-free expansion a reusable correlation primitive and shifted the bottleneck toward assumptions, local work, and seed setup.
historical_context.narrative: IKNP-style extension reduced public-key operations, yet the parties still exchanged data proportional to the number of expanded transfers. Pseudorandom correlation generators define a stronger interface: compact correlated seeds are established once, then each party expands locally to obtain a large correlated output. The paper gives efficient constructions including silent OT. The atomic contribution is this seed-to-correlation abstraction and its communication shift, not a claim that all preprocessing becomes free. It mattered because MPC designers could replace bandwidth-heavy correlation distribution with local computation and study PCGs independently across OT, vector OLE, and multiplication-preprocessing applications.

metadata.title: A Note on the Communication Complexity of Multiparty Computation in the Correlated Randomness Model
versions: revised 2020-01-02 as a minor revision of the EUROCRYPT 2019 paper
metadata.review_scope: ePrint 2018/465 PDF downloaded 2026-10-11: abstract and §1-§1.3 (PDF pp. 1-6), the paragraph on layered circuits in §1.4 (PDF p. 6), §1.5 (PDF p. 7), §2.1 (PDF p. 8), §3 with the network model, Theorems 1, 3 and 5, Corollaries 2, 4 and 6 and Lemma 8 (PDF pp. 8-10), Theorem 11 (§5, PDF p. 18) and §6 (PDF pp. 18 and 20), read for the open question, the layered-circuit protocol and its setting; proofs not audited; no separate contribution record.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: A Note on the Communication Complexity of MPC in the Correlated Randomness Model

sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes
sections.content: Locators refer to the ePrint PDF downloaded on 2026-10-11, which states no date. Printed page numbers equal PDF page numbers. Earlier ePrint versions stated a different security scope; this version is used here.

sections.heading: Main claims
sections.content: N parties communicate over a synchronous authenticated broadcast channel, and a trusted dealer gives them correlated random coins independent of the inputs before the protocol starts (abstract, PDF p. 1; §3, PDF p. 8). Theorem 1 (§3.1, PDF p. 9): for every N-party functionality computed by a layered Boolean or arithmetic circuit of size s with n inputs and m outputs, and every integer k, there is a perfectly secure protocol against semi-honest parties, without an honest majority, with communication \( n + N(m + \lceil s/k \rceil) \) and \( n/N + (m + \lceil s/k \rceil)(2^{2^k}+1) \) correlated random bits or field elements per party. Taking \( k = \log\log s \) gives communication \( O(n + N(m + s/\log\log s)) \) with polynomial storage (Corollary 2), namely \( O(s^2/\log\log s) \) (§1.1, PDF p. 3). The protocol cuts the circuit into chunks of k consecutive layers and evaluates each chunk, a local function of the previous chunk's last layer, with one-time truth tables in the style of MPC-PAPER-2013-IKMOP (§1.2, PDF pp. 3-4); the author credits the techniques behind its core lemma to earlier lookup-table protocols (§1.3, PDF pp. 5-6). Variants cover function-independent preprocessing with communication \( O(s/\log\log\log s) \) (Theorem 3 and Corollary 4) and narrow layered circuits (Theorem 5 and Corollary 6). For layered Boolean circuits, Theorem 11 (§5, PDF p. 18) gives statistical security against malicious adversaries adaptively corrupting up to \( N-1 \) parties, with additive communication \( N\kappa \). The protocols do not evaluate the circuit gate by gate, so they do not contradict the lower bound of MPC-PAPER-2016-DNPR (§1.2, PDF p. 5).

sections.heading: Open-question provenance
sections.content: The abstract (PDF p. 1) calls the construction of protocols with o(s) communication wide open for information-theoretic MPC in the correlated-randomness model, where all known protocols communicate O(s) in the online phase. Section 1 (PDF p. 2) motivates the model by secure computation without an honest majority, whose online phase correlated randomness makes information-theoretic, and takes up the question that MPC-PAPER-2016-DNPR left open. Section 6 (PDF p. 18) asks as Question 1 whether the protocols extend to non-layered circuits and calls the generalization to all circuits an interesting open question; Questions 2 and 3 (PDF pp. 18 and 20) ask for better sublinearity and for sublinear communication with linear storage. These support sublinear communication with trusted correlated randomness.

sections.heading: Historical role
sections.content: It names sublinear communication with trusted correlated randomness open and settles the layered case.

sections.heading: Limitations and unresolved review
sections.content: The protocols cover layered circuits and circuits layered by blocks of depth \( o(\log\log s) \) (§6, PDF p. 18). The correlated randomness can be cut from \( O(s^2/\log\log s) \) to slightly superlinear in s at the cost of a factor c in the \( s/\log\log s \) term of the communication (§1.1, PDF p. 3). The proofs were not audited.

metadata.review_scope: IEEE Xplore PDF of the S&P 2019 paper (pp. 1220-1237), read in full on 2026-10-12 for the application areas and workloads it names for general-purpose MPC (§I, pp. 1220-1221), its description of information-theoretic honest-majority protocols (§III-B, p. 1223), its statement that it does not benchmark performance (§V-E, p. 1227), its accounts of Sharemind and PICCO (§VI-H and §VI-I, pp. 1230-1231) and its call for standard benchmarks (§VII-C, pp. 1231-1232); the framework tables and the appendix code samples were not checked entry by entry; no separate contribution record.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: SoK: General Purpose Compilers for Secure Multi-Party Computation

sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes
sections.content: Locators use the printed page numbers of the IEEE S&P 2019 proceedings (pp. 1220–1237). The survey covers eleven frameworks with a major update since 2014: EMP-toolkit, Obliv-C, ObliVM, TinyGarble, Wysteria, ABY, SCALE-MAMBA, Sharemind, PICCO, Frigate and CBMC-GC (abstract and §IV, pp. 1220 and 1224).

sections.heading: Main claims
sections.content: The survey compares the frameworks on usability, expressiveness and cryptographic back end, by implementing three small programs in each (multiplying three inputs, an inner product and a cross-tabulation), and publishes containers that run them (§I, p. 1221; §V-B, pp. 1225–1226). It records no new protocol or bound.

sections.heading: Scope boundary
sections.content: The introduction names application areas for general-purpose MPC: secure statistical analysis, financial oversight, biomedical computation and satellite collision detection (§I, p. 1220). It states that modern implementations evaluate secure regressions on tens to hundreds of thousands of observations with tens to hundreds of variables, citing other work for these figures (§I, p. 1221). It gives no latency, communication or cost budget for any of these scenarios, and §V-E (p. 1227) states that the survey does not benchmark performance, because its sample programs are not practical use cases and frameworks with different protocol families and threat models are not directly comparable. Section VII-C (pp. 1231–1232) asks the community for a standard set of benchmark problems and metrics, which did not exist.

sections.heading: Security boundary
sections.content: Information-theoretic protocols such as BGW avoid public-key operations but need an honest majority (§III-B, p. 1223). Sharemind runs a three-server protocol on additive secret shares over a fixed ring (§VI-H, p. 1230), and PICCO uses an information-theoretic multiplication protocol with custom primitives for other operations, for any number of parties with an honest majority (§VI-I, p. 1231). The survey does not state whether these frameworks as a whole are unconditionally secure, and it reports no measurement of either.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.content: The framework descriptions reflect the versions available in 2018 and the authors' experience with them; the survey is not a performance study.

nodes.title: Incremental distributed point functions share one non-zero tree path with keys linear in the input length
nodes.subtitle: Lightweight Techniques for Private Heavy Hitters
nodes.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2021
nodes.summary: An incremental DPF secret-shares, between two servers, the values on the nodes of a depth-n binary tree whose only non-zero nodes lie on one root-to-leaf path. BBCGI21 construct one from a pseudorandom generator with key size λ + (λ+2)n + Σ_j ⌈log|G_j|⌉ bits and evaluation on an ℓ-bit prefix costing Σ_{i≤ℓ} (1 + ⌈log|G_i|/λ⌉) PRG calls (Proposition 1), whereas one standard DPF per tree level gives key size and all-prefix evaluation quadratic in n (§6).

metadata.title: Incremental distributed point functions share one non-zero tree path with keys linear in the input length
metadata.statement: An incremental DPF secret-shares, between two servers, the values on the nodes of a depth-n binary tree whose only non-zero nodes lie on one root-to-leaf path. BBCGI21 construct one from a pseudorandom generator with key size λ + (λ+2)n + Σ_j ⌈log|G_j|⌉ bits and evaluation on an ℓ-bit prefix costing Σ_{i≤ℓ} (1 + ⌈log|G_i|/λ⌉) PRG calls (Proposition 1), whereas one standard DPF per tree level gives key size and all-prefix evaluation quadratic in n (§6).

historical_context.prior_boundary: Distributed point functions compactly shared a vector with one non-zero entry, but sharing every prefix of a client string needed one DPF key per tree level, so key size and all-prefix evaluation grew quadratically in the string length (§5.2, PDF p. 10; §6, PDF p. 11).
historical_context.technical_delta: Extends the Boyle–Gilboa–Ishai DPF with one extra PRG expansion and one correction word in the level's output group per level, so a single key pair yields shares of the value on every prefix of the special point (§6, PDF p. 12).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The paper's comparison for 256-bit strings lists keys of about 6.2 KB instead of 543 KB and 513 instead of 32,640 AES operations (Table 6, PDF p. 12), which let each client send a single short message for a prefix-tree search.
historical_context.narrative: A distributed point function lets a client split a vector with a single non-zero entry into two short keys, one per server. The private heavy-hitters search of Boneh, Boyle, Corrigan-Gibbs, Gilboa, and Ishai needs shares of every prefix of each client's string, and one standard DPF per prefix length makes keys and all-prefix evaluation quadratic in the string length. Their incremental DPF shares the values on all nodes of one root-to-leaf path of a binary tree with a single key pair. It adds one PRG expansion and one correction word per level to the Boyle–Gilboa–Ishai DPF, so key size and evaluation grow linearly. For 256-bit strings their comparison lists keys of about 6.2 KB instead of 543 KB. The construction is for two servers; the paper notes that more servers would need better multiparty DPFs.

source_locator.primary_source: ePrint 2021/017 (2023-03-23 revision), §5.2 'New tool: Incremental DPF', PDF p. 10; §6, Table 6 and Proposition 1, PDF pp. 11-12; Appendix C.1 definition, PDF p. 17; Appendix C.3 proof of Proposition 1, PDF pp. 18-19; §1 limitation on k servers, PDF p. 3

qualifiers: Two keys, one per server; security means that either key alone hides the special point and the path values (§5.2, PDF p. 10).
Instantiated with a PRG G from λ to 2λ+2 bits; output groups G_1, ..., G_n are chosen per level (Proposition 1, PDF p. 12).
Table 6 uses λ = 127, 62-bit groups at inner levels, and a 2^(2λ)-size group at the leaves, which the extractability analysis needs (PDF p. 12).
limitations: The paper states that extending the approach to k servers with k − 1 malicious would need better multiparty DPFs or a different approach (§1, PDF p. 3).
The mechanism gives privacy of client keys only; protection against malformed client keys comes from the separate sketching check and the extractability analysis.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: One key for every prefix Standard DPF keys already grow linearly in the input length. The change here is that a single key pair covers all n prefix lengths, instead of one key pair per prefix length.

nodes.title: Two-server check that shared client vectors have weight at most one, private against a malicious server
nodes.subtitle: Lightweight Techniques for Private Heavy Hitters
nodes.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2021
nodes.summary: Two servers holding additive shares of a client vector in F^m check that it is a 0/1 vector with at most one non-zero entry, keeping client privacy against one malicious server up to additive attacks (Proposition 2) and without extra servers or extra client interaction. The client also shares the vector scaled by a secret random κ ∈ F together with correlated randomness; the servers take three inner products with a random sketch vector and evaluate a degree-2 check in two rounds of 4 log|F| bits per server, and an invalid vector is accepted with probability at most 2/|F| (Claim C.1).

metadata.title: Two-server check that shared client vectors have weight at most one, private against a malicious server
metadata.statement: Two servers holding additive shares of a client vector in F^m check that it is a 0/1 vector with at most one non-zero entry, keeping client privacy against one malicious server up to additive attacks (Proposition 2) and without extra servers or extra client interaction. The client also shares the vector scaled by a secret random κ ∈ F together with correlated randomness; the servers take three inner products with a random sketch vector and evaluate a degree-2 check in two rounds of 4 log|F| bits per server, and an invalid vector is accepted with probability at most 2/|F| (Claim C.1).

historical_context.prior_boundary: Sketching checks for DPF-shared vectors either protected client privacy only against semi-honest servers, or needed client-to-server communication linear in the vector length, extra rounds of client interaction, or extra non-colluding servers (§4.1, PDF p. 6).
historical_context.technical_delta: Adds a κ-scaled copy of the client vector as an authenticated randomized encoding and evaluates the verification polynomial with client-supplied correlated randomness that extends Beaver triples, following Boyle–Gilboa–Ishai, so that a server's additive attack yields only random or predictable output (§4.2, PDF p. 7).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: DPF-based aggregation gained a validity check private against a malicious server for about 3 log|F| extra amortized bits per client and server and 4 log|F| bits of server-to-server communication over two rounds (§4.2, PDF p. 7); the paper states that it immediately improves earlier advertising and messaging systems (§1, PDF p. 2).
historical_context.narrative: In DPF-based aggregation the servers must confirm that each client's shared vector has a single entry equal to one, or one client can distort the result. The sketching check of Boyle, Gilboa, and Ishai protected privacy only against semi-honest servers, and checks that tolerated a malicious server needed longer client messages, extra rounds with the client, or extra servers. Boneh and coauthors have the client also share the vector multiplied by a secret random scalar, an authenticated encoding inspired by malicious-secure MPC, and supply correlated randomness that extends Beaver multiplication triples to the verification polynomial. A server that shifts its inputs then sees only random or predictable output, while an invalid vector passes with probability at most 2/|F|. Correctness against a malicious server is not provided.

source_locator.primary_source: ePrint 2021/017 (2023-03-23 revision), §4.1, PDF p. 6; §4.2 'New tool: Malicious-secure sketching', PDF pp. 6-7; Appendix C.4 protocol, Claim C.1 and Proposition 2, PDF pp. 19-21; §2.3 remark on correctness, PDF p. 4

qualifiers: Two servers; the client supplies the correlated randomness, and security is stated for an honest client (§4.2, PDF p. 7).
Privacy against a malicious server holds up to additive offsets on the inputs and output of the client-aided computation (Proposition 2, PDF p. 20).

Soundness against a malicious client rests on the Schwartz–Zippel lemma over a prime field F (Claim C.1, PDF p. 20); Poplar's implementation uses a 62-bit field at inner levels and a 255-bit field at the leaves (§8, PDF p. 13).
limitations: Correctness of the output against a malicious server is not provided (§2.3, PDF p. 4).
Poplar's implementation uses a slightly less efficient variant of the check (§4.2, footnote 1, PDF p. 7).
The check alone does not stop a client whose keys evaluate to one at several points outside the queried set; the paper adds the extractable-DPF analysis for that (§4.1 and §4.3, PDF pp. 6 and 8).

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Privacy, not correctness, against a malicious server The scaled copy turns any shift a malicious server applies into output masked by the client's secret scalar. The servers can still corrupt the final aggregate; the paper treats that as outside its threat model.

nodes.subtitle: Three Halves Make a Whole? Beating the Half-Gates Lower Bound for Garbled Circuits
nodes.summary: RR21 constructs garbling for general Boolean circuits with free XOR gates and 1.5λ + 5 bits per AND gate using slicing and dicing, under the RTCCR hash assumption in Theorem 3. A gate-hiding variant costs 1.5λ + 10 bits per non-free gate; both have leading coefficient 1.5.

metadata.title: Three-Halves garbles a Free-XOR-compatible AND gate in 1.5λ + 5 bits
metadata.statement: RR21 constructs garbling for general Boolean circuits with free XOR gates and 1.5λ + 5 bits per AND gate using slicing and dicing, under the RTCCR hash assumption in Theorem 3. A gate-hiding variant costs 1.5λ + 10 bits per non-free gate; both have leading coefficient 1.5.

historical_context.prior_boundary: Half-gates attained two ciphertexts per AND gate and was optimal in the earlier linear-garbling model; smaller isolated gates did not preserve the input/output correlation needed for composition.
historical_context.technical_delta: Slicing labels and randomizing control information escapes the linear model while preserving the global Free-XOR offset across gates.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The result reduced composable AND-gate communication and sharpened the question of optimality in broader symmetric-key models.
historical_context.narrative: Half-gates reduced communication to two ciphertexts per AND gate while keeping XOR gates free. Its matching lower bound applied to a linear model, not every possible use of symmetric cryptography. Rosulek and Roy step outside that model by slicing wire labels and randomizing the evaluator's control information. Unlike earlier smaller isolated gates, their output labels retain the correlation needed to continue evaluating an arbitrary circuit. The result is a concrete gate-size improvement, not a universal reduction in local computation or complete protocol cost. Their optimality question subsequently motivated broader lower-bound models.

source_locator.primary_source: ePrint 2021/749, §1.1 (p. 2), §5.4 Theorem 3 (pp. 18–21), §6.1 (pp. 22–23), §8 (p. 25); PDF page numbers match printed pages

qualifiers: λ here is the manuscript's κ; XOR gates remain free and labels retain the common global offset.
The theorem uses randomized tweakable circular correlation robustness (RTCCR), not an arbitrary PRF assumption.
Gate-hiding and ordinary AND variants differ in their constant additive control cost.
limitations: The 1.5λ term is an upper bound achieved by this construction, not a universal lower bound.
Input encoding, output decoding, OT, and malicious-security enforcement are not included in a per-AND gate size.

sections.heading: Atomic contributions
sections.content: The paper presents Poplar, a system in which two non-colluding servers learn the strings held by more than t clients, or the counts of a server-chosen set of strings, from one message per client (abstract and §2, PDF pp. 1–4). Two of its mechanisms are presented as reusable beyond this application (§1, PDF pp. 1–3) and are recorded separately: MPC-CONTRIB-2021-POPLAR-INCREMENTAL-DPF: incremental distributed point functions (§5.2, PDF p. 10; §6, Table 6 and Proposition 1, PDF pp. 11–12; Appendix C.1–C.3, PDF pp. 17–19). MPC-CONTRIB-2021-POPLAR-MALICIOUS-SKETCHING: a two-server check that shares encode a vector of weight at most one, private against a malicious server (§4.2, PDF pp. 6–7; Appendix C.4, Claim C.1 and Proposition 2, PDF pp. 19–21). Not recorded as separate contributions: the extractability analysis of the public-parameter Boyle–Gilboa–Ishai DPF in the random-oracle model (§4.3, Definition 1 and Lemma 4.1, PDF p. 8; Lemma D.2, PDF p. 22), which the paper combines with the sketching check to stop double voting; the subset-histogram and heavy-hitters protocols themselves (§§4–5); and the differentially private variant (§7 and Appendix E).

sections.heading: Boundary
sections.content: Privacy holds against one malicious server colluding with any number of malicious clients; correctness against a malicious server is not provided and is left for future work (§2.3, PDF p. 4). The heavy-hitters protocol reveals the set of heavy prefixes and their counts beyond the output (§5.1, PDF p. 9). The paper states that the approach does not scale efficiently to k servers with k − 1 malicious (§1, PDF p. 3). The reported measurements are context, not portable benchmarks: with one 32-core server in each of two U.S. data centers, collecting 256-bit strings held by more than 0.1% of 400,000 clients took 3,226 s in total (Table 9, PDF p. 13; the abstract rounds this to 54 minutes). The DPF predecessors the mechanisms build on (Gilboa–Ishai 2014; Boyle–Gilboa–Ishai 2015, 2016 and TCC 2019) have no MPC records, so no lineage edge is drawn.

nodes.summary: Every functionality represented by a Boolean circuit of size S and depth D has a four-round statistically secure MPC protocol with GOD against static active rushing unbounded corruption of t < n/2 parties, with error 2^(-κ) and running time polynomial in κ, 2^n, S and 2^D, in the source's secure-channel and broadcast model.

metadata.title: Four-round statistical MPC with GOD and exponential depth-dependent work
metadata.statement: Every functionality represented by a Boolean circuit of size S and depth D has a four-round statistically secure MPC protocol with GOD against static active rushing unbounded corruption of t < n/2 parties, with error 2^(-κ) and running time polynomial in κ, 2^n, S and 2^D, in the source's secure-channel and broadcast model.

historical_context.prior_boundary: General statistical MPC at the honest-majority threshold was feasible, and four rounds were necessary, but the matching round upper bound was not known.
historical_context.technical_delta: The construction attains four rounds while retaining statistical security and GOD; its running time remains exponential in n and circuit depth.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The exact interaction bound is separated from the still-open efficiency of constant-round information-theoretic general computation.
historical_context.narrative: Statistical MPC already allowed an honest majority to compute general functions with guaranteed output delivery, but its exact number of rounds remained unsettled. Applebaum, Kachlon and Patra achieve the four-round bound for general functionalities. The result is about interaction, not polynomial efficiency: its work is polynomial in the circuit size but exponential in circuit depth and the number of participants. Keeping those dependencies visible separates a resolved round-feasibility question from the remaining task of making constant-round information-theoretic computation efficient. The paper explicitly notes that eliminating the depth dependence is open even under much weaker, passive corruption conditions.

source_locator.primary_source: ePrint 2023/418 revision 2025-06-17, §1 model (p. 5), §1.1.3 and Theorem 1.5 with following discussion and footnote 3 (p. 8)

qualifiers: Static active rushing computationally unbounded adversary; t < n/2.
Secure point-to-point channels and broadcast; four rounds in that model.
Running time poly(κ, 2^n, S, 2^D); statistical error 2^(-κ).
limitations: This is not polynomial-time MPC for arbitrary polynomial-size circuits or growing n.
The NC¹ efficiency discussion has a qualified extension via secure reductions from log space; it is not a universal impossibility outside NC¹.
No adaptive-corruption or practical-performance claim is admitted.

metadata.title: F4-OLE PCGs give near-linear communication for multiparty Boolean triples
metadata.statement: FOLEAGE constructs multiparty Boolean-triple preprocessing from an F4-OLE pseudorandom correlation generator, with communication near linear in the number of parties times the number of triples plus lower-order seed terms.

historical_context.prior_boundary: Silent PCGs reduced communication for correlation expansion, but efficient actively secure multiparty preprocessing over the binary field retained costly party-scaling and correlation-conversion bottlenecks.
historical_context.technical_delta: FOLEAGE specializes PCG machinery to F4-OLE and derives Boolean multiplication triples with communication dominated by the party-by-triple term, supplemented by lower-order seed setup.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: It advanced the concrete and asymptotic preprocessing frontier for multiparty Boolean circuits without reclassifying the optimization as merely an implementation.
historical_context.narrative: Pseudorandom correlation generators showed how short seeds could replace large communicated correlation batches, but multiparty Boolean preprocessing still had to manage active security and unfavorable scaling across parties. FOLEAGE builds its preprocessing around a PCG for multiplication over the four-element field and converts that structure into Boolean multiplication triples. The normalized cost is near linear in parties times generated triples, with additional lower-order seed terms stated separately. The atomic contribution is this F4-OLE-based correlation protocol and its communication boundary, not the accompanying code alone. It mattered because the PCG line reached a sharper multiparty binary-MPC design point suitable for implementation study.

historical_context.prior_boundary: Honest-majority protocols usually optimized total communication or assumed comparable links, so one weak path could throttle an otherwise low-bandwidth multiplication protocol.
historical_context.technical_delta: The paper gives communication variants that route latency-critical and bulk messages over different links while retaining the three- and five-element totals of Trio and Quad.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: It made link topology an explicit protocol-design coordinate rather than leaving heterogeneous-network handling to an implementation after the security protocol was fixed.
historical_context.narrative: Low total communication does not guarantee high throughput when a protocol puts latency-critical or bulk traffic on the weakest links. HP-MPC treats that placement as part of protocol design. Its Trio and Quad variants redirect messages so that all but two links may be arbitrarily bandwidth-limited and all but one may have arbitrarily high latency, while retaining the paper's total communication per multiplication. The mapped contribution is this topology-aware scheduling boundary across the exact passive three-party and malicious four-party configurations. Vectorized local work, the complete masked-sharing protocols, the repository revision, and reported throughput are recorded separately rather than folded into one generic claim of speed.

historical_context.prior_boundary: Communication-efficient honest-majority protocols could still become computation-bound because each secure gate expanded into many local additions, multiplications, hashes, or pseudorandom values.
historical_context.technical_delta: The revised masked-sharing correlations remove local arithmetic from the multiplication path without paying additional communicated ring elements in the three- or four-party configuration.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: It made per-gate instruction count a protocol-level optimization target alongside rounds and communication, before any compiler or hardware measurement was considered.
historical_context.narrative: Honest-majority MPC papers often compared communicated elements while treating local share arithmetic as negligible. At the throughput reached by batched ring and Boolean evaluation, however, those additions and multiplications can become the bottleneck. HP-MPC changes the correlations in Trio and Quad's masked shares so their gate protocols require up to half the basic local instructions of the related baselines discussed in the paper, without increasing the three- and five-element communication totals. This is a protocol-level efficiency result. Vectorization helps realize it, but the pinned implementation and the billion-gate measurements are separate evidence objects with their own version, hardware, network, and batch boundaries.

historical_context.prior_boundary: Existing high-throughput honest-majority protocols already reached low communication, but their sharing correlations and local arithmetic left distinct computation and topology bottlenecks.
historical_context.technical_delta: Trio changes the masked shares held by the two online parties, while Quad adds a fourth party and compare-view checks to verify the resulting messages against one malicious corruption.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The paper introduced two complete security-specific protocol configurations whose sharing semantics support its later local-work and heterogeneous-link optimizations.
historical_context.narrative: Prior three- and four-party ring protocols already had attractive communication totals, so HP-MPC did not present another generic replicated-sharing row. Trio changes which masked values and mask shares the online parties retain, arranging multiplication so input-dependent and input-independent errors can be corrected with three communicated ring elements. Quad builds on that sharing layout with a fourth party and compare-view checks, tolerating one malicious corruption with five elements per multiplication. This card records the two complete, security-specific protocol constructions. Their local-instruction savings, weak-link schedules, software revision, and measured throughput remain separate research or engineering objects.

metadata.statement: With n = 3t+1 and synchronous private authenticated channels, the current CDPP manuscript gives statistically secure MPC with GOD and O(D) expected rounds against malicious adaptive unbounded corruption; for Θ(n^7) parallel evaluations of a circuit with c_M multiplication gates, one field-element input per party and one common output, total communication is O(c_M n^7+n^8) field elements.

historical_context.prior_boundary: Low-communication statistical protocols could use abort or incur additional round costs; combining robustness with O(D) rounds required more expensive primitives.
historical_context.technical_delta: Robust authenticated packed sharing, VSS and degree reduction support GOD with constant per-gate amortized communication across a large SIMD batch.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: Low amortized communication and guaranteed completion are obtained together, leaving general single-circuit computation and smaller batch sizes as explicit residuals.
historical_context.narrative: Detecting a malformed sharing can permit a protocol to abort, but guaranteed output delivery requires the computation to survive that behavior. Choudhury, Damgård, Patil and Patra build robust primitives for packed secret sharing and use them in statistical MPC. The current manuscript combines O(D) expected rounds with constant amortized communication at n = 3t+1. That amortization requires Θ(n^7) evaluations of the same circuit in parallel, and its theorem also includes an n^8 input/output term. The result therefore approaches the low-communication GOD target from the batching direction; removing the large SIMD requirement remains a separate question.

qualifiers: n = 3t+1; malicious adaptive rushing computationally unbounded adversary; statistical security with GOD.
Synchronous private authenticated channels; broadcasts are included or emulated with constant expected round protocols.
Θ(n^7) independent SIMD evaluations; O(c_M n^7+n^8) field elements, not O(c_M) total for one execution.
Source field convention has |F| >= 2^κ and symbols of O(κ) bits for polynomial-size circuits and party counts; constant overhead is in field elements, not constant bits independent of security.
limitations: O(D) is an expected round bound, not a deterministic worst-case bound.
General-circuit-to-SIMD compilation introduces a log |C| size factor and potentially a depth-dependent additive term for irregular circuits.
The current revision is synchronous; an older abstract's asynchronous claims are not admitted.
No constant local-computation overhead or measured practicality claim is admitted.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Statistical GOD with large-batch amortization The unit of comparison is the full SIMD workload, including the n^8 term in Theorem 7.1, not just an online multiplication in isolation. The source's §1.3 asks to reduce that batch or handle a general circuit without its cost.

historical_context.prior_boundary: Three-Halves escaped the earlier linear-garbling bound; later lower bounds still imposed restrictions on algebraic representations.
historical_context.technical_delta: Model the joint distribution of labels, gate data and oracle responses using Shannon-type information inequalities, restricting oracle-query behavior rather than the internal algebra.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The result matches the leading Three-Halves cost in a broader but still explicitly bounded single-gate model.
historical_context.narrative: Three-Halves showed why optimality in a fixed algebraic template need not imply optimality for garbling generally. Januzelli, Rosulek and Roy instead derive information inequalities from a single gate's security and oracle behavior. Their theorem matches the Three-Halves leading cost without prescribing the internal algebra of the algorithms. It still requires non-adaptive evaluator queries and knowledge of which input evaluations share each query, together with a stronger security game and composable label correlations. Those conditions are part of the result, not technical details that can be dropped when comparing a different construction.

source_locator.primary_source: ePrint 2025/876, §1.1 (pp. 3–4), Definitions 12–14 (pp. 9–10), §3.3 and Definition 16 (pp. 11–12), Theorem 26 and Corollary 27 (p. 23); PDF page numbers match printed pages

qualifiers: Minicrypt adversaries are computationally unbounded with polynomially many random-oracle queries.
The garbler receives input labels and chooses output labels; all labels have λ bits and the same Free-XOR correlation.
Strong security reveals complementary labels only after the adversary loses oracle access.
Non-adaptivity and coordination restrict Ev, not Gb.
limitations: Does not cover adaptive or uncoordinated evaluator oracle queries.
Does not establish a whole-circuit lower bound for non-projective or layer-batched encodings.
Strong security is not silently replaced by ordinary garbling security.

metadata.title: Active CRT-based MPC keeps leading computation and communication linear with abort
metadata.statement: For any fixed 0 < ε < 1/2 and fields with log |F| = Ω(n² log n), BEP gives statistically secure MPC with abort for general arithmetic circuits against t < (1/2−ε)n active corruptions, with O(|C| log |F|) leading communication and bit-computation cost under the source convention suppressing statistical-security, log n and log log |F| factors.

historical_context.prior_boundary: Leading linear communication was known for active security with abort, while jointly leading linear communication and computation was available for passive CRT-based MPC.
historical_context.technical_delta: Active consistency mechanisms extend CRT-based computation to active security with abort while preserving its leading cost dependence.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The source separates the cost of active checking from the further problem of continuing to guaranteed output delivery.
historical_context.narrative: Constant-leading communication does not automatically give low local work: previous active protocols could still pay a factor proportional to the number of participants in computation. CRT-based secret sharing had reduced both leading costs for passive security. Bienstock, Escudero and Polychroniadou extend that approach to active security with abort. Their arithmetic-circuit theorem preserves the large-field restriction and suppresses statistical-security and logarithmic factors in its cost notation. It does not guarantee that honest parties receive an output after detected cheating. Accordingly, the result is a neighboring cost benchmark for guaranteed-delivery research, not a solution to the GOD target.

qualifiers: Active corruption t < (1/2−ε)n for any fixed positive ε; statistical security with abort.
Large fields with log |F| = Ω(n² log n).
The source explicitly suppresses λ, log n and log log |F| factors; the leading O(|C| log |F|) expression is not a bound uniform in all parameters.
The circuit-cost discussion counts multiplication gates; additions can be local.
limitations: Guaranteed output delivery is not provided.
No small-field, adaptive-corruption or exact O(D)-round claim is normalized from this introductory theorem.
Constant overhead with guaranteed output delivery for a single general circuit is not claimed.

nodes.title: Stacked garbling whose input-routing cost no longer scales with branches times input length
nodes.subtitle: Suffix-Invariant Programmable PRFs and Applications to Stacked Garbling
nodes.summary: GHJY26 Theorem 10 gives a garbling scheme from black-box one-way functions that selects one of B = 2^n = poly(λ) Boolean branches of size C with a common I-bit input, with total garbled size O(I log B·λ + Bλ + Cλ) bits and O(B log B) garbler and evaluator time, and the same correctness and security guarantees as LogStack, whose garbled size is O(BIλ + Cλ). The demultiplexer is a garbled programmer for a short-key offline-online suffix-invariant programmable PRF (Theorem 8 and Lemma 3).

metadata.title: Stacked garbling whose input-routing cost no longer scales with branches times input length
metadata.statement: GHJY26 Theorem 10 gives a garbling scheme from black-box one-way functions that selects one of B = 2^n = poly(λ) Boolean branches of size C with a common I-bit input, with total garbled size O(I log B·λ + Bλ + Cλ) bits and O(B log B) garbler and evaluator time, and the same correctness and security guarantees as LogStack, whose garbled size is O(BIλ + Cλ). The demultiplexer is a garbled programmer for a short-key offline-online suffix-invariant programmable PRF (Theorem 8 and Lemma 3).

historical_context.prior_boundary: Stacked garbling (Heath–Kolesnikov 2020; LogStack 2021) reduced branch material to O(Cλ) from one-way functions but kept an additive O(BIλ) demultiplexer term, so it helped little when branches were light and inputs large.
historical_context.technical_delta: Recast the demultiplexer as one-point programming of a pseudorandom function, define suffix-invariant programmable PRFs, construct a short-key offline-online one from black-box one-way functions for polynomial-size domains, and garble only its short online programming step.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The input-routing term becomes O(I log B·λ) while LogStack's O(B log B) computation is kept, because suffix invariance limits each inactive branch to log B possible garbage outputs.
historical_context.narrative: Stacked garbling lets a garbler send material proportional to one branch when a circuit selects one of B branches, but LogStack still paid O(BIλ) bits to route an I-bit input to every candidate branch, so the savings faded when branches were light and inputs large. Goyal, Heath, Jain, and Yang recast this routing step as programming a pseudorandom function at one hidden point. They define suffix-invariant programmable PRFs, build a version with short online keys from one-way functions for polynomial-size domains, and garble only its programming step. The resulting scheme has garbled size O(I log B·λ + Bλ + Cλ) and keeps LogStack's O(B log B) work, because suffix invariance limits each inactive branch to log B possible garbage outputs. The size of an individual garbled gate is unchanged.

source_locator.primary_source: ePrint 2026/815 (2026-07-02 revision), §1.1 Theorem 1 (informal) and concrete comparison, PDF p. 5; Theorem 2 (informal), PDF p. 6; §2.3 suffix invariance and garbage collection, PDF p. 11; §6.2 Theorem 8 and Lemma 3, PDF p. 26; §7.1 Theorem 9, PDF pp. 30–31; §7.2 Theorem 10, PDF p. 33; Appendix E Theorem 14, PDF p. 54. PDF pages are printed pages plus three.

qualifiers: The number of branches is polynomial, B = 2^n ≤ poly(λ); the programmable PRF is constructed only for polynomial-size domains (Theorem 2, PDF p. 6).
Branches share one interface {0,1}^I → {0,1}; the paper notes that stacked garbling supports multiple outputs but analyses one (footnote 5, PDF p. 29).
Theorem 10 is the black-box construction with garbled size O(nIλ + Bλ + Cλ), n = log B. The off-the-shelf variant of Theorem 9 is non-black-box and has garbled size O(nI·poly(λ) + Bλ + Cλ).

Security is correctness, authenticity, obliviousness, and privacy in the Bellare–Hoang–Rogaway garbling framework (Theorem 14, PDF p. 54); the proofs of Theorems 13 and 14 are sketches that reuse LogStack's simulators (PDF pp. 50 and 54).
The additive O(Bλ) term remains; the tailored online key carries a candidate-seed tree of size O(B) that replaces LogStack's separate seed-delivery gadget (§7.2, PDF p. 32).

The concrete comparison is analytic: the dominant communication term is 4BIλ bits for LogStack and 8I log B·λ bits here, comparable for B = 2, 4 and smaller for every B ≥ 8 (PDF p. 5), up to lower-order terms.
limitations: The circuit term O(Cλ) is inherited from the base Yao scheme (point-and-permute, or free XOR and half gates under a circular correlation-robust hash; Appendix E, PDF p. 53); the result does not bear on the single-gate question MPC-OP-016.
No implementation or measurement is reported.
The suffix-invariant programmable PRF, the adaptive programmable PRF from one-way functions (§5.4), and the PRF/DPF equivalences (Theorems 4–6) are not recorded as separate contributions.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Input routing, not gate size Stacked garbling already avoids paying for every branch's gates. This result removes the remaining product of the number of branches and the input length from the garbled size; the additive Bλ term and the circuit term remain.

nodes.title: PRF-based multiparty scalar-vector triples with exponential party-dependent key cost
nodes.subtitle: Compressing Correlations via Secret Replication: PCFs from Symmetric Cryptography
nodes.summary: IKR construct a k-party PCF for additive shares of a scalar x, vector a, and xa using only PRFs; if each scalar share lies in a common support S, each party holds k|S|^(k−1)−(k−1)|S|^(k−2)+2k−2 PRF keys and evaluates each key once per coordinate.

metadata.title: PRF-based multiparty scalar-vector triples with exponential party-dependent key cost
metadata.statement: IKR construct a k-party PCF for additive shares of a scalar x, vector a, and xa using only PRFs; if each scalar share lies in a common support S, each party holds k|S|^(k−1)−(k−1)|S|^(k−2)+2k−2 PRF keys and evaluates each key once per coordinate.

historical_context.prior_boundary: Two-party VOLE does not immediately supply consistently programmable cross-terms with privacy against colluding receivers.
historical_context.technical_delta: Secret projection of several lines with shared slopes and independent intercepts supplies the multiparty scalar-vector correlation.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The construction establishes symmetric-only feasibility while making party-dependent local work and storage explicit.
historical_context.narrative: Moving from two-party VOLE to multiparty scalar-vector products requires compatible cross-terms without exposing a sender's vector to colluding receivers. Reusing a single line is unsafe because receivers can combine evaluations to recover its slope. IKR instead use several lines with a shared slope and independent intercepts, together with secret projection and replicated PRF keys. The resulting correlation provides additive shares of a scalar, a vector, and their product, with local indexed evaluation and privacy against any strict coalition. This extends symmetric-only correlation generation to a multiparty setting, but the key count grows exponentially with the participants. That construction cost motivates a scaling problem rather than establishing a universal lower bound or a complete malicious MPC protocol.

source_locator.primary_source: ITC 2026 proceedings, Theorem 2, p. 7:6; Definition 6, pp. 7:8–7:9; §4.2 and Corollary 27, pp. 7:14–7:17; Definitions 12–13, pp. 7:10–7:11

qualifiers: The correlation shares one scalar across all vector coordinates and offers indexed random access.
Insider security concerns every fixed strict coalition, including k−1 exposed keys, relative to the corruptible ideal correlation.
Formal Corollary 27 uses a joint scalar-share support X subset F^k and its union S of marginal supports.
limitations: Exponential dependence on k remains even when F=S=F2.
Adaptive evaluation indices do not establish adaptive party corruption, malicious distributed key generation, or UC composition.
This atom is unauthenticated SVMT; authenticated variants have additional parameters and are not folded into its guarantee.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Multiparty scalar-vector correlation Catalogue-only inclusion records the exact result; the source asks in §6 whether its party-count cost is inherent. The source proves a correlation mechanism; it does not establish that the mechanism's exponential cost is necessary for every symmetric construction.

metadata.title: Secret projection recovers small-scalar VOLE PCFs from PRFs
metadata.statement: IKR derive a two-party PCF for VOLE over a finite field F with scalar in X subset F from any PRF; the direct construction assigns |X| keys to the sender and |X|−1 to the receiver, with one PRF call per held key per evaluated coordinate.

historical_context.prior_boundary: Small-domain VOLE PCFs from symmetric primitives were already known from Roy and subsequent work.
historical_context.technical_delta: A secret projection of a linear correlation gives a common explanation of this two-party construction and the later multiparty construction.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The mechanism separates attainable correlation types from the stronger assumptions used in general OT and OLE expansion.
historical_context.narrative: Small-domain VOLE already admitted constructions from symmetric primitives. IKR revisit that result by viewing a line's evaluations as a linear correlation: the sender receives enough evaluations to recover the line, while the receiver receives one secretly selected evaluation. Replicated PRF keys compress these correlations and provide local access to vector coordinates. This perspective explains an existing construction within the same framework used for the paper's multiparty results. It also exposes the remaining parameter boundary: evaluation work grows with the scalar domain, even when keys can be compressed. The contribution is this unifying mechanism, not first VOLE feasibility or a construction of independent random OT correlations from arbitrary one-way functions.

source_locator.primary_source: ITC 2026 proceedings, Theorem 1, p. 7:5; Corollary 22 and Remarks 24–25, p. 7:14; Definitions 12–13, pp. 7:10–7:11

qualifiers: VOLE shares one scalar across the vector; it is not a batch of independent random OTs.
The finite field and scalar domain are distinct parameters; the stated evaluation cost is linear in |X|.
The result concerns correlated keys and local evaluation, not a free distributed setup.
limitations: Large scalar domains make the direct evaluation expensive; key compression alone does not remove this evaluation cost.
No generic OWF-based random-OT PCG or complete malicious MPC protocol is established by this contribution.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Small-scalar VOLE via secret projection The sender holds vectors a,b; the receiver holds one scalar x and ax+b. The scalar persists across evaluated vector coordinates. Catalogue-only inclusion supports the open-question comparison without adding a research-map node.

nodes.title: Layer-batched ROM garbling separates circuit-size cost from statistical error
nodes.subtitle: Breaking the Ω(|C|κ) Barrier on Garbled Circuit Size in the Random Oracle Model
nodes.summary: LS26 Theorem 1 gives Boolean-circuit garbling of size O(|C| log T + Dκ² log T) bits and input encoding O(WI log T) bits in the programmable random-oracle model, with error 2^(−κ) against a computationally unbounded T-query adversary; D is depth and WI is the number of input wires.

metadata.title: Layer-batched ROM garbling separates circuit-size cost from statistical error
metadata.statement: LS26 Theorem 1 gives Boolean-circuit garbling of size O(|C| log T + Dκ² log T) bits and input encoding O(WI log T) bits in the programmable random-oracle model, with error 2^(−κ) against a computationally unbounded T-query adversary; D is depth and WI is the number of input wires.

historical_context.prior_boundary: Practical gatewise constructions paid a security-parameter factor per AND gate, while finer lower bounds addressed restricted single-gate interfaces.
historical_context.technical_delta: Encode inputs non-projectively and garble batches of gates within a layer rather than independently preserving the earlier gate interface.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The construction separates whole-circuit amortization from single-gate optimality and exposes a remaining depth-dependent overhead.
historical_context.narrative: Lower bounds for an isolated gate do not automatically constrain a construction that encodes inputs and layers jointly. Li and Song exploit that distinction in the random-oracle model, separating the adversary's query budget from the requested statistical error. Their garbled-circuit size has a circuit-linear term depending on log T and an additional depth-dependent term. The improvement is asymptotic and depends on the parameter regime; it is not an unconditional concrete-speed claim. This gives an important boundary when reading the single-gate optimality question: the new construction avoids that interface rather than disproving a theorem within it.

source_locator.primary_source: ePrint 2026/1297, §1.1 Theorem 1 and Corollary 1 (pp. 4–5), §1.2 (pp. 7–8), §3.4 Definition 1 (pp. 16–17); PDF page numbers match printed pages

qualifiers: T bounds adversary oracle queries; κ specifies statistical error. They are different coordinates.
The stated upper bound yields o(|C|κ) when log T = o(κ) and Dκ log T = o(|C|); these are sufficient conditions, not a lower bound excluding other regimes.
Input encoding is non-projective; the bound is not a per-single-AND-gate claim or a Free-XOR guarantee.
The random oracle is programmable, not a global or non-programmable oracle.
limitations: The work explicitly defers improved concrete size; no measured implementation advantage is claimed here.
The input-encoding term remains separate and is not omitted from full communication accounting.
This different interface is not an APPROACHES edge to the single-gate question MPC-OP-016.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.content: Whole-circuit cost, not single-gate cost The depth term and the separation of T from κ are essential to this result. Taking log T = Θ(κ) does not give a sub-κ leading cost per gate.

metadata.title: Suffix-Invariant Programmable PRFs and Applications to Stacked Garbling
versions: revised 2026-07-02 (minor revision of the CRYPTO 2026 publication; this revision read in full on 2026-10-11)

sections.heading: Atomic contribution
sections.content: MPC-CONTRIB-2026-GHJY-SIPPRF-STACKED-GARBLING records the improved stacked garbling scheme: Theorem 1 (informal, PDF p. 5), Theorem 10 (§7.2, PDF p. 33) and Theorem 14 (Appendix E, PDF p. 54), with the short-key offline-online suffix-invariant programmable PRF of §6.2 (Theorem 8 and Lemma 3, PDF p. 26) as its demultiplexer. PDF pages are three more than the printed page numbers of the ePrint revision. The paper also proves results that are not recorded as separate contributions here, because they concern pseudorandom functions and distributed point functions rather than an MPC mechanism: correctness and index hiding imply pseudorandomness under uniform programming (Theorem 4, PDF p. 19); a black-box equivalence between non-adaptive programmable PRFs and two-party distributed point functions (Theorems 5 and 6, PDF p. 22), one direction of which the paper attributes to earlier work (PDF p. 21); and adaptive programmable PRFs for polynomial-size domains from one-way functions via programmable distributed point functions (§5.4, PDF pp. 23–24; Theorem 3, PDF p. 6).

sections.heading: Boundary
sections.content: The improvement concerns the input-routing (demultiplexer) term of stacked garbling for conditional branching. It does not change the size of a garbled gate: the circuit term is inherited from the base Yao scheme, which may use free XOR and half gates (Appendix E, PDF p. 53). It therefore has no bearing on the optimal size of garbled AND gates. The paper reports no implementation; its concrete comparison with LogStack (PDF p. 5) is an analytic count of the dominant communication terms. The stacked-garbling predecessors the paper builds on, Heath–Kolesnikov (CRYPTO 2020) and LogStack (EUROCRYPT 2021), have no records yet, so no lineage edge is drawn.

sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes

sections.heading: Atomic contributions
sections.content: MPC-CONTRIB-2026-IKR-SMALL-VOLE-PCF: secret-projection derivation of the small-scalar VOLE PCF; Theorem 1, p. 7:5, and Corollary 22, p. 7:14. This revisits Roy's construction rather than claiming first feasibility. MPC-CONTRIB-2026-IKR-MULTIPARTY-SVMT-PCF: multiparty scalar-vector multiplication correlations from PRFs; Theorem 2, p. 7:6, and Corollary 27, pp. 7:16–7:17.

sections.heading: Open-question locators
sections.content: Section 1.4, p. 7:7, explicitly leaves OT PCGs from symmetric cryptography open. Section 6, p. 7:19, asks whether the scalar-size and party-count blowups of these VOLE-style constructions are inherent. These questions stay with the paper and are not listed as separate problems.

sections.heading: Security boundary
sections.content: Definitions 12–13, pp. 7:10–7:11, use corruptible ideal correlations and insider security after seed exposure. The PCF supports adaptively chosen evaluation indices; that is not a claim of adaptive party corruption. Correlated seed distribution remains a distinct setup task. These atoms do not assert an end-to-end malicious or UC MPC protocol, nor negligible-error authentication from a small authentication-key domain.

sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes
sections.content: The source is the ePrint manuscript received 2026-08-21. Its ePrint metadata describes it as a major revision of a TCC 2026 publication; this card uses the available manuscript identity and does not assign an unverified proceedings date.

sections.heading: Open-question provenance
sections.content: Section 1.1, numbered PDF page 3, explicitly identifies extending efficient constant-round information-theoretic computation to general circuits as an open question. The fall-back protocols there instantiate an information-theoretic base protocol for NC¹ and add guarantees under computational assumptions at higher corruption levels. The source's abstract alone does not make the NC¹ efficiency restriction visible. The paper is cited in the research history of efficient constant-round information-theoretic MPC.

sections.heading: Limitations and unresolved review
sections.content: This is a source/provenance-only intake: no atomic positive result, protocol configuration, map membership or lineage edge is admitted. The relevant introduction and theorem statements were checked; security proofs were not independently verified. Its phrase about extending beyond NC¹ is not interpreted as excluding all log-space functionalities, which AKP23 footnote 3 discusses via secure reductions to NC¹.
