nodes.title: Efficient information-theoretic MPC for all circuits
nodes.summary: Efficient information-theoretic MPC for all circuits

metadata.title: Efficient information-theoretic MPC for all circuits
metadata.summary: Parties with private channels evaluate any circuit with security against unbounded adversaries and no setup, with polynomial work, a constant number of rounds, and communication below the circuit size. Every known protocol gives up at least one of these.

requirements.label: All circuits, polynomial work
requirements.target: every polynomial-size Boolean circuit C, with computation and communication poly(κ, n, |C|)

requirements.label: No assumption
requirements.target: statistical security against computationally unbounded adversaries; no computational assumption or random oracle

requirements.label: No setup
requirements.target: private channels and broadcast only; no trusted dealer, correlated randomness or preprocessing

requirements.label: Constant rounds
requirements.target: a constant number of rounds, independent of the depth and size of C and of n

requirements.label: Communication below circuit size
requirements.target: total communication poly(κ, n) · (o(|C|) + input length + output length)

sources.locator: Abstract (p. 1); Theorem 1 and the remarks after its proof (pp. 2-5)
Abstract, PDF p. 1; Corollary 1, §3, PDF p. 13

frontier.assumption: none; fewer than n/2 corrupted parties
frontier.note: Every circuit is evaluated on secret shares with perfect security against fewer than n/2 passive corruptions, but rounds grow with circuit depth and every multiplication gate costs communication. Gate-by-gate protocols against Θ(n) corruptions need Ω(n·|C|) bits, which the known protocols meet up to constant factors.

Encodings of degree three whose size is tied to branching-program size give constant-round protocols with polynomial work for log-space functions; for general circuits the cost of this route grows exponentially with depth. Like every known information-theoretic protocol, they communicate at least in proportion to circuit size.

sources.locator: Theorem 1.5 and the following paragraph, §1.1.3, p. 8 (ECCC TR23-031)

frontier.assumption: none; fewer than n/2 corrupted parties
frontier.note: Four rounds for every circuit, even against active adversaries and with guaranteed output delivery, but running time polynomial in 2^D for depth D and in 2^n, so efficient only for NC¹ and n = O(log κ). The theorem bounds running time, not communication on its own.

sources.locator: Protocol 5.1 and Theorem 5.2, §5, PDF pp. 16-17; 'Bootstrapping' paragraph of §6, PDF pp. 18-19 (ePrint 2011/613)

frontier.assumption: LWE and circular security; common random string
frontier.note: Three broadcast rounds with a common random string, or two with a reusable public-key setup, against any number of corruptions. With bootstrapping, communication depends only on input and output size, at the price of a circular-security assumption.

frontier.line: One-time truth tables from a trusted dealer

sources.locator: Theorem 1, §3.1, PDF p. 9 (author draft of TCC 2013)

frontier.assumption: none; correlated randomness from a trusted dealer
frontier.note: Before the inputs are known a dealer hands out correlated randomness, and no honest majority is needed. Two rounds and communication linear in the input length need correlations exponential in the input length; with polynomial correlations, only layered circuits of size s are known to need less, O(s/log log s).

recognized_by.statement: Asks how many rounds secure evaluation of a circuit needs while keeping communication polynomial in its size, noting that the earlier non-cryptographic constant-round method blows up message size exponentially.
Calls removing the exponential dependence on depth from constant-round information-theoretic protocols a famous open problem going back to BMR90, even for one passive corruption.
Revisits whether the communication of unconditionally secure computation depends on the computational complexity of the function, and whether constant rounds suffice.

Asks whether information-theoretic protocols inherently need more communication and rounds than computationally secure ones, and calls communication much smaller than the circuit size a long-standing open problem.
Names the circuit-size barrier, that all known information-theoretic protocols communicate in proportion to the circuit complexity of the function, and asks whether it is inherent.

layers.target: every circuit, no assumption, no setup
layers.distance_note: Reached in 1988 for an honest majority, which is necessary without setup; the asymptotic ladder measures rounds and communication.

rungs.level: With half or more of the parties corrupted, some functions, such as two-party OR, have no information-theoretically secure protocol.
Every circuit, perfectly secure against fewer than n/2 passive or n/3 active corruptions, over private channels.

layers.not_applicable: Security is unconditional by definition; protocols that use a one-way function or LWE appear as near misses on the asymptotic ladder.

layers.distance_note: No protocol with polynomial work, no assumption and no setup has constant rounds or communication o(|C|) for all circuits; each is reached only by giving up one of these.

rungs.level: Gate-by-gate evaluation: rounds proportional to circuit depth, communication proportional to circuit size.

sources.locator: remarks after the proof of Theorem 1 (p. 5)

rungs.level: Gate-by-gate protocols need Ω(n) bits per multiplication gate, and ordered ones need rounds proportional to multiplicative depth.
Constant rounds with polynomial work against one passive corruption.
Constant-degree statistical randomized encodings of all circuits, which would give constant rounds.
Communication o(|C|) plus input and output length, with an honest majority.
Constant rounds with polynomial work for every circuit, with an honest majority.

near_misses.level: Log-space functions only: constant rounds with polynomial work.
Work exponential in depth and in n: four rounds for every circuit, even against active adversaries.
A one-way function: constant rounds with polynomial work, by jointly garbling the circuit.
LWE, circular security and a common random string: three rounds, communication independent of circuit size.

sources.locator: Theorem 5.2, §5, PDF p. 17; 'Bootstrapping' paragraph of §6, PDF pp. 18-19

near_misses.level: A trusted dealer with correlations exponential in the input length: two rounds, communication linear in the input.
A trusted dealer, layered circuits only: O(s/log log s) communication for size s, even without an honest majority.
A trusted dealer with polynomial correlations, all circuits, even without an honest majority: still open.

layers.not_applicable: The covered literature names applications of general-purpose MPC, such as secure regressions on tens to hundreds of thousands of records (MPC-PAPER-2019-SOK-COMPILERS, §I), but states no budget for any of them and measures no protocol that is both unconditional and free of setup: the honest-majority systems here (MPC-PAPER-2018-ABY3, MPC-PAPER-2024-HPMPC) expand pairwise pseudorandom seeds, which gives up the no-assumption requirement.

sections.heading: Why this goal
sections.content:
With an honest majority, information-theoretic protocols compute every
function without any cryptographic assumption (MPC-PAPER-1988-BGW), but they
evaluate the circuit gate by gate, so rounds grow with its depth and
communication with its size. Cryptography removes both costs: a one-way
function gives constant rounds (MPC-PAPER-1990-BMR), and LWE with circular
security gives communication independent of circuit size
(MPC-PAPER-2012-AJW). Whether security against unbounded adversaries
inherently costs more interaction and communication is the question this goal
records; MPC-PAPER-2016-DNPR calls it open and probably very hard.

sections.heading: Reading the frontier
sections.content:
Rows group protocols by technique. The randomizing-polynomial and four-round
rows reach constant rounds by restricting the functions or by paying
exponential work, the threshold-encryption row by assuming LWE and a reference
string, and the trusted-dealer row by giving up the plain model, which also
lets it tolerate a dishonest majority. The communication cells rest on the
observation that no known information-theoretic protocol without setup
communicates less than the circuit size (MPC-PAPER-2017-VAIKUNTANATHAN). The
four-round theorem bounds only running time, so its communication cell is
unknown.

nodes.title: Optimal fairness without an honest majority
nodes.summary: Optimal fairness without an honest majority

metadata.title: Optimal fairness without an honest majority
metadata.summary: With all but one party possibly corrupted, know exactly which two-party functions can be computed with complete fairness, and flip a coin in r rounds with bias O(1/r), the least Cleve's bound allows, for any constant number of parties. Each is known only in special cases.

requirements.label: All but one corrupted
requirements.target: a malicious adversary may corrupt any n − 1 of the n parties, one of two in the two-party case

requirements.label: Fair functions characterized
requirements.target: a criterion decidable from the function table says which two-party functions with finite domains and ranges admit complete fairness

requirements.label: Coin-flipping bias O(1/r)
requirements.target: r-round coin flipping with bias O(1/r) for every constant number of parties, matching the Ω(1/r) lower bound

frontier.assumption: none; fewer than n/3 malicious parties
frontier.note: With fewer than n/3 malicious parties every function is computed with full security, so every function is fair and a coin can be flipped with no bias; this needs most parties to be honest.

frontier.assumption: oblivious transfer; enhanced trapdoor permutations for more than two parties
frontier.note: Bias O(1/r) for two parties, and for a constant number of parties when fewer than two thirds are corrupted; the bias grows doubly exponentially in the gap between corrupted and honest parties, and the technique gives nothing once two thirds or more are corrupted.

sources.locator: Theorem 1.1 and the remark after it, §1.1 (arXiv 2104.08820 v2)

frontier.note: Against all but one corrupted party: bias O(√(log r)/r) for three parties, and about r^(−1/2−Θ(1)) for any constant number, which from four parties on is polynomially above 1/r.

Two parties, one corrupted. Functions without an embedded XOR are fair, and Boolean functions with a common output are characterized; for differing output bits the known sufficient and necessary conditions leave a gap, and for larger ranges only some functions are known to be fair. Coin flipping cannot be fair, so these protocols do not address its bias.

recognized_by.statement: Calls a tight characterization of the Boolean functions two parties can compute with complete fairness the most pressing question its work leaves open.
Presents itself as a step towards characterizing complete fairness for finite-domain functions and names finalizing that characterization the main open question.
Defines the characterization of fairness as a necessary and sufficient condition for a two-party function to be fair, and states that it remains open.
States that whether Cleve's lower bound on the bias of coin flipping is tight had been open for over twenty years.
Calls finding the optimal bias of coin flipping with more than two parties the main open question of the area.

layers.distance_note: A criterion is known for Boolean functions with a common output; for differing output bits known conditions leave a gap, and for larger ranges only some functions are classified.

rungs.level: Without an honest majority, coin flipping cannot be completely fair: every r-round protocol has bias Ω(1/r).

sources.locator: as stated by Moran, Naor and Segev, §1.1, PDF p. 3 (ePrint 2009/214)

rungs.level: Every function without an embedded XOR, such as AND, OR and the millionaires' problem, is completely fair.
Almost all Boolean functions whose two domains differ in size are fair, and so are some asymmetric and non-Boolean ones.
Boolean functions with a common output: fair exactly when the all-one or all-zero vector is an affine combination of rows or columns.
Boolean functions whose two parties may receive different output bits.
Every function with finite domains and ranges, each party receiving its own output.

layers.not_applicable: Every result here assumes oblivious transfer or trapdoor permutations; the open questions are which functions can be fair and how small the bias can be, not which assumption suffices.

layers.target: bias O(1/r) for any constant number of parties
layers.best: O(1/r) for two parties, worse beyond
layers.distance_note: Optimal for two parties and a √(log r) factor away for three, but from four parties on the best bias, about r^(−1/2−Θ(1)), is polynomially above 1/r.

rungs.level: Every r-round protocol in which half or more of the parties may be corrupted has bias Ω(1/r).

sources.locator: as stated by Moran, Naor and Segev, §1.1, PDF p. 3, and by Haitner and Tsfadia, §1

rungs.level: Two parties: bias O(1/r), within a factor of about two of the lower bound.
Three parties, two corrupted: bias O(log³ r/r), improved to O(√(log r)/r) in 2017.
Any constant number of parties, all but one corrupted: bias about r^(−1/2−Θ(1)), below the majority protocol's 1/√r.
With a number of parties polynomial in r, bias about 1/√r is unavoidable; for a constant number only Ω(1/r) is known.
Three parties: bias O(1/r), or a proof that the √(log r) factor is needed.
Any constant number of parties: bias within a polylogarithmic factor of 1/r.
Any constant number of parties, all but one corrupted: bias O(1/r).

near_misses.level: Fewer than two thirds corrupted: bias O(1/r) for a constant number of parties.
Fewer than three quarters corrupted: bias O(log³ r/r) for a constant number of parties.

layers.not_applicable: The covered literature describes no deployment scenario, workload or budget for fair protocols without an honest majority: the results classify which functions are fair and bound coin-flipping bias as a function of rounds, and no covered paper reports an implementation.

sections.heading: Why this goal
sections.content:
Without an honest majority a corrupted party can stop as soon as it learns
the output, and MPC-PAPER-1986-CLEVE shows that some functions, starting with
coin flipping, cannot be computed with complete fairness. Two questions
measure how much fairness survives: which functions can still be computed
completely fairly, a question MPC-PAPER-2008-GHKL opened, and, for coin
flipping, how close the bias can come to Cleve's Ω(1/r). Together they mark
the best fairness this setting allows.

sections.heading: Reading the frontier
sections.content:
Rows group protocols by technique. The honest-majority row shows what giving
up the corruption threshold buys: every function becomes fair. The
coin-flipping rows are scored on bias, since coin flipping is the standard
function that cannot be fair, and the two-party row on the characterization.
A partial cell covers a restricted number of parties or corruptions, or a
subclass of functions.

nodes.title: Garbled circuits of provably minimal size
nodes.summary: Garbled circuits of provably minimal size

metadata.title: Garbled circuits of provably minimal size
metadata.summary: Garbled circuits in which XOR gates are free and each AND gate is as small as any such scheme can be, with a lower bound that proves it. AND gates of about 1.5λ bits exist, but the matching lower bound holds only for a restricted class of schemes.

requirements.label: Free XOR, gate by gate
requirements.target: each gate is garbled on its own, all λ-bit wire labels share one global offset, and XOR gates need no ciphertext

requirements.label: Provably minimal AND gates
requirements.target: AND gates no larger than a lower bound proved for every free-XOR scheme in the random-oracle model, with arbitrary evaluator queries

frontier.note: One global offset between the two labels of every wire makes XOR gates cost nothing, so the size of a garbled circuit is set by its AND gates; later schemes made those gates smaller.

sources.locator: Abstract and half-gates construction; §7.3, Theorem 3 (p. 21) and discussion (p. 23)

frontier.note: Two λ-bit ciphertexts per AND gate, proved optimal only among linear schemes, whose algorithms are linear apart from non-adaptive oracle queries; the paper cannot rule out one-ciphertext AND gates by other means.

frontier.assumption: randomized tweakable circular correlation-robust hash function
frontier.note: 1.5λ + 5 bits per AND gate. A matching 1.5λ − negl(λ) lower bound holds only for strongly secure schemes whose evaluator makes non-adaptive, coordinated oracle queries.

O(|C| log T + Dκ² log T) bits for a whole circuit of depth D against adversaries making T oracle queries, below |C|κ for circuits wide relative to their depth. Inputs are encoded non-projectively and gates are garbled a layer at a time, so there is no single-gate size and no free-XOR guarantee.

recognized_by.locator: §7.3, discussion after Theorem 3, p. 23 (EUROCRYPT 2015 author version)
recognized_by.statement: Proves its two-ciphertext bound only for linear garbling schemes and states that it cannot rule out garbling an AND gate with a single ciphertext by other means.
Asks whether its 1.5κ-bit AND gate is optimal in a model more inclusive than linear garbling, and suggests Minicrypt as the natural setting.
Proves a matching 1.5λ bound only for evaluators whose oracle queries are non-adaptive and coordinated, and notes that these restrictions may be limiting.

layers.distance_note: Reached in 2008; the asymptotic ladder measures the AND gates that remain.

rungs.level: One global offset between wire labels makes XOR gates free; only the other gates cost ciphertexts.

layers.not_applicable: Constructions use symmetric-key hash functions and lower bounds are stated in the random-oracle model, which captures them; the open question is the size of an AND gate, not the assumption.

layers.target: AND-gate size matched by a lower bound
layers.distance_note: Construction and lower bound already meet at 1.5λ for strongly secure schemes with restricted evaluator queries; what remains is to drop those restrictions, or to beat 1.5λ by exploiting them.

rungs.level: Two λ-bit ciphertexts per AND gate.
Linear garbling schemes need two ciphertexts per AND gate.
1.5λ + 5 bits per AND gate, outside the linear model.
Strongly secure schemes with non-adaptive, coordinated evaluator queries need 1.5λ − negl(λ) bits per AND gate.
The 1.5λ bound for strongly secure schemes with arbitrary evaluator queries, or a smaller such gate.
The 1.5λ bound for every free-XOR scheme, or an AND gate below 1.5λ bits.

near_misses.level: Garbling a layer at a time: whole circuits below |C|κ bits when wide relative to their depth.

layers.not_applicable: Deployment is not the question: the goal asks for a lower bound matching an AND-gate size already counted exactly in bits on the asymptotic ladder, and the covered garbling papers describe no deployment scenario, workload or budget that such a bound, or a smaller gate, would be measured against.

sections.heading: Why this goal
sections.content:
In garbled-circuit two-party computation the garbled circuit is what one
party sends, and once XOR gates are free the garbled AND gates determine that
communication (MPC-PAPER-2008-FREEXOR). Each step down in AND-gate size has
been followed by a lower bound for the class of schemes it uses, and the area
asks where constructions and lower bounds meet for every free-XOR scheme
built from symmetric-key primitives (MPC-PAPER-2015-HALFGATES,
MPC-PAPER-2021-THREE-HALVES, MPC-PAPER-2025-JRR-GARBLING-BOUNDS).

sections.heading: Reading the frontier
sections.content:
Rows are schemes that garble one gate at a time, except the last, which
garbles a layer of gates together and so falls outside the single-gate
question; it shows what giving up per-gate garbling with free XOR buys. A
minimality cell is yes only when a construction is matched by a lower bound
for every free-XOR scheme; partial marks a match for a restricted class of
schemes, or a smaller whole-circuit size with no lower bound.

nodes.title: Efficient constant-round information-theoretic MPC for general circuits
nodes.summary: Efficient constant-round information-theoretic MPC for general circuits

metadata.title: Efficient constant-round information-theoretic MPC for general circuits
metadata.summary: Can unconditionally secure MPC evaluate every polynomial-size circuit in a constant number of rounds with polynomial work? Known constant-round information-theoretic protocols cost exponentially in circuit depth, or are efficient only for log-space functions.

profile.Functionality: all polynomial-size Boolean circuits
profile.Security: passive (semi-honest), static
profile.Assumption: none: statistical security against unbounded adversaries
profile.Efficiency: constant rounds; polynomial computation and communication
profile.Model: private channels and broadcast; no setup or preprocessing
profile.Setting: honest majority, t < n/2

named_open_by.statement: Asks how many rounds are needed to evaluate a circuit securely while keeping communication polynomial in its size, noting that the earlier non-cryptographic constant-round method blows up message size exponentially; it answers the question only by assuming a one-way function.

Observes that all known constant-round information-theoretic protocols depend exponentially on circuit depth and calls removing this dependency, even for a passive adversary with t = 1, a famous open problem going back to BMR90.

metadata.resolution_condition: A uniform protocol family with a statistical simulation proof, for n parties with private authenticated channels and broadcast and a static passive adversary corrupting t < n/2 of them, that evaluates every polynomial-size Boolean circuit C in an absolute constant number of rounds (independent of the depth and size of C and of n), with total computation and communication poly(kappa, n, |C|), counting all setup and preprocessing, and with no computational assumption, random oracle, or trusted correlated randomness.

sections.heading: Background
sections.content:
Honest-majority protocols in the style of MPC-PAPER-1988-BGW compute any
function with information-theoretic security, but they evaluate the circuit
gate by gate, so their number of rounds grows with its depth. Constant-round
protocols instead represent the function by a randomized encoding of low
algebraic degree, which secret-sharing protocols can evaluate in a few rounds
(MPC-PAPER-2000-IK). Without cryptographic assumptions, the known encodings
have polynomial size only for functions with small branching programs, so for
general circuits their cost grows exponentially with depth.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
Consider n parties connected by private authenticated channels and a broadcast
channel, and a static passive adversary corrupting t < n/2 of them. Is there a
protocol family that evaluates every polynomial-size Boolean circuit \( C \)
with statistical security against computationally unbounded adversaries, in a
constant number of rounds that depends neither on \( C \) nor on n, with
computation and communication polynomial in the security parameter
\( \kappa \), in n and in \( |C| \)? No computational assumption and no trusted
setup or preprocessing may be used.

sections.heading: Why it is open
sections.content:
With a one-way function the question is settled: MPC-PAPER-1990-BMR has the
parties jointly garble the circuit in [a constant number of
rounds](MPC-OP-009). Without cryptography no statistically private garbling of
general circuits is known. The known information-theoretic constant-round
route evaluates a randomized encoding of the function, and the perfect and
statistical encodings known have polynomial size only for branching programs
(MPC-PAPER-2000-IK, MPC-PAPER-2017-APPLEBAUM-RE), which is why [log-space
functions](MPC-OP-006) are settled. For a circuit of depth D the cost of this
route is exponential in D. MPC-PAPER-2023-AKP settles the round complexity at
four rounds even against active adversaries, but with [running time exponential
in depth and in the number of parties](MPC-OP-007), and states that removing the
depth dependence is open even for [a single passive
corruption](MPC-OP-008). [Polynomial-size statistical encodings of constant
degree for all circuits](MPC-OP-010) would suffice.

sections.heading: What would not resolve it
sections.content:
- A constant-round protocol that uses a random oracle or any computational
  assumption.
- A protocol whose setup or preprocessing is exponential in depth, or an
  efficient protocol only for a restricted class such as NC¹ or log-space.
- A protocol with polynomial work whose round count grows with depth, even
  slowly.

sections.heading: Formal target
sections.content:
Fix n parties, static passive corruption of t < n/2 of them, synchronous private
authenticated point-to-point channels, and broadcast. For every polynomial-size
Boolean circuit \( C \), require statistical simulation security against
computationally unbounded adversaries with error negligible in \( \kappa \), an
absolute constant number of rounds independent of the depth and size of
\( C \) and of n (which may grow polynomially with \( \kappa \)), and total
local computation and communication, including any setup and preprocessing, of

\[
\mathrm{poly}(\kappa, n, |C|).
\]

Computational assumptions, random oracles, and trusted correlated randomness are
excluded. Active security, an optimal round count, adaptive corruption, and
guaranteed output delivery are not required.

sections.heading: Known obstacles
sections.content:
The known constant-round route encodes the computation in a form whose size can
grow exponentially with depth, and no statistically private replacement for
the computational garbling of MPC-PAPER-1990-BMR is known. This is a limitation
of known constructions, not a lower bound. NC¹ is not the boundary of what is
efficient: MPC-PAPER-2023-AKP notes (footnote 3) that log-space functions reduce
to NC¹ functions by non-interactive secure reductions.

sections.heading: Research history
sections.content:
MPC-PAPER-1990-BMR asked how many rounds secure evaluation of a circuit needs
with polynomial communication, and answered it with a one-way function by
jointly garbling the circuit. MPC-PAPER-2000-IK introduced randomizing
polynomials, low-degree randomized encodings whose size is tied to branching
program size, giving constant-round information-theoretic protocols for those
functions; MPC-PAPER-2017-APPLEBAUM-RE surveys perfect encodings of degree three
for arithmetic branching programs. MPC-PAPER-2023-AKP settled four-round
statistical MPC with guaranteed output delivery at t < n/2 with work polynomial
in \( 2^D \) and \( 2^n \), separating round feasibility from efficiency. In
2026, the fall-back-secure protocols of MPC-PAPER-2026-IT-CONSTANT-ROUND still
build on efficient information-theoretic base protocols for NC¹.

nodes.title: The 1.5λ bound for strongly secure gates with unrestricted queries
nodes.summary: The 1.5λ bound for strongly secure gates with unrestricted queries

metadata.title: The 1.5λ bound for strongly secure gates with unrestricted queries
metadata.summary: The garbled-gate lower bound required only for schemes meeting the strong security notion of Januzelli, Rosulek and Roy, with no restriction on evaluator queries. Open.

profile.Functionality: one AND gate garbled compatibly with free XOR, λ-bit labels
profile.Efficiency: lower bound of 1.5λ − negl(λ) bits per garbled gate
profile.Model: random-oracle model (Minicrypt); arbitrary evaluator queries
profile.Setting: only schemes that are strongly secure (complementary labels revealed after oracle access ends)

named_open_by.statement: Proves the bound for strongly secure gates only under non-adaptive, coordinated evaluator queries and notes that these restrictions may be limiting.

metadata.resolution_condition: A proof of the 1.5*lambda - negl(lambda) bound for every strongly secure (JRR25 Definition 16) free-XOR single-gate scheme with no restriction on evaluator queries, or a strongly secure scheme in exactly this model with smaller gates. Removing only one of the two query restrictions does not settle it.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
Keep the single-gate setting of MPC-PAPER-2025-JRR-GARBLING-BOUNDS: the garbler
receives the input wire labels and chooses the output labels, all labels have
\( \lambda \) bits and share one free-XOR offset, and security is their strong
notion, which reveals the complementary labels only after the adversary loses
oracle access. Remove both restrictions on the evaluator: its oracle queries
may depend on earlier answers, and it need not know which other input
combinations share each query. Does every such scheme still need
\( 1.5\lambda - \mathrm{negl}(\lambda) \) bits per garbled gate?

sections.heading: Why it is open
sections.content:
MPC-PAPER-2025-JRR-GARBLING-BOUNDS proves the bound in exactly this setting
except that [evaluator queries are non-adaptive and
coordinated](MPC-OP-017), and its §1.1 notes that these restrictions may be
limiting. An extended proof has to justify its information inequalities without
them, while a smaller gate would have to exploit adaptive or uncoordinated
queries; neither has appeared. Here adaptivity refers to the evaluator's oracle
queries, not to adaptive choice of inputs.

nodes.title: Constant-round information-theoretic MPC for log-space functions
nodes.summary: Constant-round information-theoretic MPC for log-space functions

metadata.title: Constant-round information-theoretic MPC for log-space functions
metadata.summary: Constant-round information-theoretic MPC with polynomial work, for functions with polynomial-size branching programs. Solved by randomizing polynomials of degree three.

profile.Functionality: functions with polynomial-size branching programs (log-space)
profile.Security: passive (semi-honest), static
profile.Assumption: none: statistical security against unbounded adversaries
profile.Efficiency: constant rounds; polynomial computation and communication
profile.Model: private channels and broadcast; no setup or preprocessing
profile.Setting: honest majority, t < n/2

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
For functions given by branching programs of polynomial size, which include
NC¹ and non-uniform log-space, give a constant-round protocol with statistical
security against a passive adversary corrupting t < n/2 parties, with work
polynomial in the branching program size.

sections.heading: Resolution
sections.content:
MPC-PAPER-2000-IK shows that every function can be randomized by polynomials
of degree three whose size is tied to its branching program size, and reduces
secure evaluation of any function to secure evaluation of degree-three
polynomials, which honest-majority protocols do in a constant number of rounds.
For functions with polynomial-size branching programs this gives
constant-round information-theoretic protocols with polynomial communication.
MPC-PAPER-2017-APPLEBAUM-RE (Theorem 4.1 and §5.1) presents the perfect
degree-three encodings of arithmetic branching programs and the resulting
constant-round protocols for Boolean and arithmetic log-space functions.
MPC-PAPER-2023-AKP (footnote 3) notes that its four-round protocol also extends
from NC¹ to log-space functions by non-interactive secure reductions.

nodes.title: Four-round statistical MPC with work exponential in depth
nodes.summary: Four-round statistical MPC with work exponential in depth

metadata.title: Four-round statistical MPC with work exponential in depth
metadata.summary: Constant-round information-theoretic MPC when running time may grow exponentially with circuit depth and the number of parties. Solved in four rounds, even against active adversaries.

profile.Functionality: all polynomial-size Boolean circuits
profile.Security: passive (semi-honest), static
profile.Assumption: none: statistical security against unbounded adversaries
profile.Efficiency: constant rounds; running time polynomial in κ, |C|, 2^D and 2^n
profile.Model: private channels and broadcast; no setup or preprocessing
profile.Setting: honest majority, t < n/2

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
Give a constant-round protocol for every polynomial-size Boolean circuit with
statistical security against a static adversary corrupting t < n/2 parties,
where the running time may be polynomial in \( \kappa \), the circuit size,
\( 2^D \) for depth D, and \( 2^n \).

sections.heading: Resolution
sections.content:
MPC-PAPER-2023-AKP proves that every functionality can be computed in four
rounds with statistical security against an active, static, rushing,
computationally unbounded adversary corrupting t < n/2 parties, with error
\( 2^{-\kappa} \) and running time \( \mathrm{poly}(\kappa, 2^n, s, 2^d) \) for a
circuit of size s and depth d. The security includes guaranteed output
delivery, and four rounds are known to be optimal in this setting. The protocol
is efficient only for NC¹ functions and \( n = O(\log \kappa) \); the paragraph
after the theorem separates the remaining efficiency question from this round
bound.

nodes.title: Constant-round information-theoretic MPC against one passive corruption
nodes.summary: Constant-round information-theoretic MPC against one passive corruption

metadata.title: Constant-round information-theoretic MPC against one passive corruption
metadata.summary: Constant-round information-theoretic MPC for all circuits with polynomial work, when only one party is passively corrupted, as with three parties. Open: even here no constant-round protocol avoids cost exponential in depth.

profile.Functionality: all polynomial-size Boolean circuits
profile.Security: passive (semi-honest), static
profile.Assumption: none: statistical security against unbounded adversaries
profile.Efficiency: constant rounds; polynomial computation and communication
profile.Model: private channels and broadcast; no setup or preprocessing
profile.Setting: a single corrupted party (t = 1, n ≥ 3)

named_open_by.statement: States that getting rid of the exponential dependence on depth is open even in weaker models, giving a passive adversary with resiliency t = 1 as the example.

metadata.resolution_condition: A protocol family for some fixed n >= 3 (or all n >= 3) tolerating one static passive corruption that evaluates every polynomial-size Boolean circuit with statistical security in a constant number of rounds and polynomial computation and communication, without computational assumptions or trusted setup.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
With n ≥ 3 parties of which only one may be passively corrupted, is there a
protocol that evaluates every polynomial-size Boolean circuit with statistical
security in a constant number of rounds and with polynomial computation and
communication, without computational assumptions or trusted setup?

sections.heading: Why it is open
sections.content:
MPC-PAPER-2023-AKP names this case explicitly: removing the exponential
dependence on depth is open even for a passive adversary and resiliency t = 1.
A single corruption does not remove the obstacle of the general case. The
known constant-round route evaluates a randomized encoding of the function, and
the perfect or statistical encodings known have polynomial size only for
branching programs (MPC-PAPER-2000-IK), so for deep circuits its cost is still
exponential in depth.

nodes.title: Constant-round MPC from one-way functions
nodes.summary: Constant-round MPC from one-way functions

metadata.title: Constant-round MPC from one-way functions
metadata.summary: Constant-round MPC for all circuits with polynomial work, when security may rest on a one-way function. Solved by having the parties jointly garble the circuit.

profile.Functionality: all polynomial-size Boolean circuits
profile.Security: passive (semi-honest), static
profile.Efficiency: constant rounds; polynomial computation and communication
profile.Model: private channels and broadcast; no setup or preprocessing
profile.Setting: honest majority, t < n/2

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
Give a protocol that evaluates every polynomial-size Boolean circuit among n
parties with an honest majority in a constant number of rounds, with polynomial
computation and communication, assuming only a one-way function.

sections.heading: Resolution
sections.content:
MPC-PAPER-1990-BMR gives a protocol for n parties, a majority of them honest,
that evaluates any circuit in a constant number of rounds with a polynomial
amount of communication, over private channels with broadcast and assuming any
one-way function. It tolerates a polynomial-time adversary that corrupts parties
dynamically. The parties use interaction to build a common garbled circuit,
which each then evaluates locally. The garbling is where computational
security enters, so the result leaves the information-theoretic question open.

nodes.title: Constant-degree statistical randomized encodings for all circuits
nodes.summary: Constant-degree statistical randomized encodings for all circuits

metadata.title: Constant-degree statistical randomized encodings for all circuits
metadata.summary: Polynomial-size perfect or statistical randomized encodings of constant degree for every polynomial-size circuit. Constant-degree encodings can be evaluated in constant rounds, so this would give constant-round information-theoretic MPC for all circuits.

profile.Functionality: randomized encodings of constant algebraic degree for all polynomial-size circuits
profile.Security: perfect or statistical privacy
profile.Efficiency: encoding size polynomial in circuit size

named_open_by.locator: §3.2, paragraph after Theorem 3.4, p. 10, and §6, p. 31 (ECCC TR17-067)
named_open_by.statement: Calls efficient perfect or statistical decomposable encodings for general polynomial-size circuits, or even for circuits of depth about log squared, wide open, and asks the same for constant algebraic degree.

metadata.resolution_condition: For every polynomial-size Boolean circuit, a randomized encoding of constant algebraic degree over some finite field, computable in polynomial time, of size polynomial in the circuit size, with perfect or statistical privacy and efficient decoding and simulation.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
Is there, for every polynomial-size Boolean circuit, a randomized encoding of
constant algebraic degree and polynomial size whose privacy is perfect or
statistical? Such an encoding is a randomized function of the input and fresh
random bits whose output reveals the circuit's value and nothing else.
Securely computing a function reduces to computing its encoding, and an
encoding of constant degree can be computed in a constant number of rounds
with information-theoretic security (MPC-PAPER-2017-APPLEBAUM-RE, §5.1, p. 29),
so a positive answer would give [constant-round information-theoretic MPC for
all circuits](MPC-OP-001).

sections.heading: Why it is open
sections.content:
Perfect encodings of degree three are known for arithmetic branching programs
(MPC-PAPER-2017-APPLEBAUM-RE, Theorem 4.1), building on MPC-PAPER-2000-IK, and
polynomial-size circuits have encodings of degree three only with computational
privacy, from one-way functions computable in NC¹ (Theorem 4.2 there).
MPC-PAPER-2017-APPLEBAUM-RE calls even efficient perfect or statistical
encodings for circuits of depth \( \log^2 n \) wide open, and asks for nontrivial
lower bounds.

nodes.title: Information-theoretic MPC with communication sublinear in circuit size
nodes.summary: Information-theoretic MPC with communication sublinear in circuit size

metadata.title: Information-theoretic MPC with communication sublinear in circuit size
metadata.summary: Can unconditionally secure MPC communicate asymptotically less than the size of the circuit it evaluates? Without trusted setup, every known information-theoretic protocol communicates in proportion to circuit size, while LWE-based protocols do not.

profile.Functionality: all polynomial-size Boolean circuits
profile.Security: passive (semi-honest), static

sections.heading: Background
sections.content:
In information-theoretic MPC with an honest majority, protocols in the style of
MPC-PAPER-1988-BGW evaluate the circuit gate by gate on secret shares, and each
multiplication gate costs communication. Without trusted correlated
randomness, every known information-theoretic protocol communicates at least in
proportion to the circuit size, a limitation called the circuit-size barrier
(MPC-PAPER-2017-VAIKUNTANATHAN). Computational protocols escape it: threshold
fully homomorphic encryption based on LWE, with a circular-security assumption,
gives communication that depends only on the input and output length
(MPC-PAPER-2012-AJW).

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
Consider n parties with private channels, an honest majority t < n/2, and a
static passive adversary. Is there a protocol that computes every
polynomial-size Boolean circuit \( C \) with statistical security against
unbounded adversaries and polynomial computation, while communicating
\( o(|C|) \) bits plus a term polynomial in \( \kappa \) and n times the input
and output length? No computational assumption, trusted setup, or correlated
randomness may be used.

sections.heading: Why it is open
sections.content:
The efficient information-theoretic protocols all follow the gate-by-gate
pattern, and MPC-PAPER-2016-DNPR proves that such protocols need
\( \Omega(n) \) bits for every multiplication gate, so a sublinear protocol must
abandon that pattern. MPC-PAPER-2004-IK ties closely related questions about the
communication of information-theoretic MPC to information-theoretic private
information retrieval and short locally decodable codes, themselves
long-standing open problems. The analogous question [without an honest
majority but with a trusted dealer of correlated randomness](MPC-OP-012) is
also open for general circuits; there it is settled only for [layered
circuits](MPC-OP-013), with [exponentially large correlated
randomness](MPC-OP-014), or [under LWE and circular security](MPC-OP-015).

sections.heading: What would not resolve it
sections.content:
- Protocols based on LWE, DDH, LPN, or any other computational assumption.
- Protocols that rely on trusted correlated randomness or a preprocessing
  phase, unless the correlations are themselves generated information
  theoretically within the same communication bound.
- Constant-factor savings, such as communicating a fixed fraction of the gate
  count.
- Sublinear communication only for a restricted class of circuits.

sections.heading: Formal target
sections.content:
Fix n parties, static passive corruption of t < n/2 of them, and synchronous
private authenticated channels, with no setup. For every polynomial-size Boolean
circuit \( C \) with input length \( \ell_{\mathrm{in}} \) and output length
\( \ell_{\mathrm{out}} \), require statistical simulation security against
unbounded adversaries with error negligible in \( \kappa \), computation
\( \mathrm{poly}(\kappa, n, |C|) \), and total communication

\[
\mathrm{poly}(\kappa, n) \cdot \bigl( g(|C|) + \ell_{\mathrm{in}} + \ell_{\mathrm{out}} \bigr)
\quad \text{for some } g(s) = o(s).
\]

Computational assumptions, random oracles, and correlated randomness are
excluded. Active security and constant rounds are not required.

sections.heading: Known obstacles
sections.content:
MPC-PAPER-2016-DNPR shows that gate-by-gate protocols, in which every gate
output is held as a fresh secret sharing, need \( \Omega(n) \) bits per
multiplication gate, with an honest majority and, for additive output sharing,
with preprocessing and a dishonest majority. In the correlated-randomness
model, MPC-PAPER-2013-IKMOP gives evidence that communication linear in the
input length may require super-polynomial correlated randomness. These rule out
particular approaches, not every protocol.

sections.heading: Research history
sections.content:
The gate-by-gate protocols of MPC-PAPER-1988-BGW fixed the pattern of
communication per multiplication gate. MPC-PAPER-2004-IK asked whether the
communication of unconditionally secure computation must depend on the
function's computational complexity and related it to private information
retrieval. Threshold fully homomorphic encryption removed the dependence under
LWE and a circular-security assumption (MPC-PAPER-2012-AJW), and
MPC-PAPER-2013-IKMOP removed it with exponential
correlated randomness. MPC-PAPER-2016-DNPR proved the per-gate lower bound for
gate-by-gate protocols, and MPC-PAPER-2017-VAIKUNTANATHAN restated the question
as the circuit-size barrier. MPC-PAPER-2019-COUTEAU gave the first sublinear
protocol in the correlated-randomness model, for layered circuits.

sections.heading: Background
sections.content:
In the correlated-randomness model a trusted dealer, before the inputs are
known, gives each party a random string drawn from a joint distribution; in
practice an input-independent preprocessing phase plays the dealer's role.
Correlated randomness makes information-theoretic security possible without an
honest majority, which the plain model rules out, and protocols in this model
are among the most efficient known (MPC-PAPER-2013-IKMOP;
MPC-PAPER-2019-COUTEAU). As in plain-model information-theoretic MPC, where
[the same question](MPC-OP-011) is asked for an honest majority, every known
protocol for general circuits with polynomial correlated randomness
communicates in proportion to the circuit size.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
Consider \( n \ge 2 \) parties, any \( n-1 \) of which may be corrupted by
a static passive adversary, and suppose a trusted dealer, before the inputs
are known, gives them correlated random strings of polynomial size. Is there
then an information-theoretic protocol that computes every polynomial-size
Boolean circuit \( C \) with communication \( o(|C|) \) plus a term
polynomial in \( \kappa \) and n times the input and output length, with
polynomial computation?

sections.heading: Why it is open
sections.content:
Correlated randomness makes gate-by-gate protocols cheap and removes the need
for an honest majority, but their online communication is still linear in the
circuit size (MPC-PAPER-2019-COUTEAU). MPC-PAPER-2013-IKMOP makes communication
linear in the input length using one-time truth tables of exponential size and
gives evidence that super-polynomial correlated randomness may be necessary for
that communication. MPC-PAPER-2019-COUTEAU obtains \( O(s/\log\log s) \) for
layered circuits of size s, and for circuits layered by blocks of depth
\( o(\log\log s) \), and leaves general circuits open. Putting a general
circuit in layered form can multiply its size by up to its depth, so the bound
is not sublinear in the original size. Under LWE and a circular-security
assumption, threshold fully homomorphic encryption avoids the question
computationally ([communication independent of circuit
size](MPC-OP-015)).

sections.heading: What would not resolve it
sections.content:
- Protocols for a restricted class of circuits, such as layered circuits.
- Correlated randomness or computation of super-polynomial size.
- Protocols that rely on a computational assumption.
- Protocols that tolerate only a minority of corrupted parties.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
In the correlated-randomness model, compute every layered Boolean circuit of
size s, one whose gates split into layers with every wire joining adjacent
layers, with information-theoretic security and communication \( o(s) \) plus
input and output terms.

sections.heading: Resolution
sections.content:
MPC-PAPER-2019-COUTEAU gives the first generic protocol in the
correlated-randomness model whose communication is sublinear in circuit size.
For a layered Boolean or arithmetic circuit of size s with N parties, input
length \( \ell_{\mathrm{in}} \) and output length \( \ell_{\mathrm{out}} \), it
is perfectly secure against semi-honest parties without an honest majority,
communicates \( O(\ell_{\mathrm{in}} + N(\ell_{\mathrm{out}} + s/\log\log s)) \),
and uses correlated randomness polynomial in s. It cuts the
circuit into chunks of \( \log\log s \) consecutive layers and evaluates each
chunk with one-time truth tables, the technique of MPC-PAPER-2013-IKMOP. For
Boolean circuits the protocol extends to statistical security against
malicious adversaries.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
In the correlated-randomness model, with no bound on the size of the
correlations, compute every functionality with information-theoretic security
and communication sublinear in circuit size.

sections.heading: Resolution
sections.content:
MPC-PAPER-2013-IKMOP realizes every multiparty functionality without an honest
majority in two rounds, with perfect security against passive parties and total
communication linear in the total input length. With two parties, the dealer
hands out one-time truth tables: additive shares of the function's table with
rows and columns shifted by random offsets, so the correlated randomness grows
exponentially with the input length. A variant gives statistical security
with abort against malicious parties. The paper gives evidence that
super-polynomial correlated randomness may be inherent for this communication.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
With a trusted setup and computational security under LWE and a
circular-security assumption, compute every polynomial-size circuit with
communication sublinear in its size.

sections.heading: Resolution
sections.content:
MPC-PAPER-2012-AJW has the parties generate a joint key for threshold fully
homomorphic encryption under LWE, evaluate the circuit homomorphically, and
decrypt jointly. With the leveled scheme, secure under LWE, communication is
proportional to the number of multiplicative levels of the circuit; with
bootstrapping, which needs a circular-security assumption for the basic
LWE-based scheme, communication depends only on the input and output size. The
protocol takes three rounds with a common random string, or two with a reusable
public-key setup, and is secure against malicious adversaries corrupting any
number of parties. A trusted dealer can supply the common random string. The
circuit-dependent work is a local homomorphic evaluation.

named_open_by.locator: §7.3, Discussion after Theorem 3, p. 23 (EUROCRYPT 2015 author version)
named_open_by.statement: Proves its two-ciphertext bound only for linear garbling schemes and states that it cannot rule out garbling an AND gate with a single ciphertext by other means.
Asks whether its 1.5κ-bit AND gate is optimal in a model more inclusive than linear garbling, and suggests Minicrypt as the natural setting.
Proves a matching 1.5λ bound only for evaluators whose oracle queries are non-adaptive and coordinated, and notes that these restrictions may be limiting.

metadata.resolution_condition: Either a proof that every garbling scheme for a single AND gate with lambda-bit labels sharing one free-XOR offset, secure against unbounded adversaries with polynomially many random-oracle queries and with no restriction on evaluator queries, has garbled gates of at least 1.5*lambda - negl(lambda) bits; or a secure scheme in exactly this model with smaller garbled gates.

sections.heading: Background
sections.content:
In a garbled circuit one party encrypts each gate so that another can evaluate
the circuit on hidden inputs, and when XOR gates are free the garbled AND gates
determine the communication (MPC-PAPER-2008-FREEXOR). Half-gates garbles an AND
gate with two \( \lambda \)-bit ciphertexts and is optimal among linear schemes
(MPC-PAPER-2015-HALFGATES), and three-halves garbling leaves the linear model
to reach about \( 1.5\lambda \) bits while keeping free XOR
(MPC-PAPER-2021-THREE-HALVES). Lower bounds are stated in the random-oracle
model against unbounded adversaries, which captures schemes built only from
symmetric-key primitives.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
In the random-oracle model, against computationally unbounded adversaries that
make polynomially many oracle queries, does every secure garbling scheme for a
single AND gate that is compatible with free XOR, with \( \lambda \)-bit labels
sharing one global offset, produce garbled gates of at least
\( 1.5\lambda - \mathrm{negl}(\lambda) \) bits? The evaluator's queries may be
adaptive and need not be coordinated across input combinations. A proof
answers the question, and so does a secure scheme in this model with smaller
gates.

sections.heading: Why it is open
sections.content:
MPC-PAPER-2015-HALFGATES proves two ciphertexts necessary only for linear
schemes, whose algorithms are linear apart from non-adaptive oracle queries,
and three-halves garbling shows that leaving the linear model helps.
MPC-PAPER-2025-JRR-GARBLING-BOUNDS derives the matching \( 1.5\lambda \) bound
from information inequalities without assuming linearity, but only for schemes
meeting a stronger security notion and only when [evaluator queries are
non-adaptive and coordinated](MPC-OP-017). [The same bound for strongly secure
schemes with arbitrary queries](MPC-OP-005) is already open. A proof has to
control what an adaptive evaluator learns from oracle answers, and a smaller
gate would have to exploit exactly such queries.

sections.heading: What would not resolve it
sections.content:
- Beating the half-gates cost of \( 2\lambda \), which three-halves garbling
  already does.
- Smaller isolated gates obtained by changing the input or output label
  correlations, which gives up composition with free XOR.
- Weakening security to authenticity alone (privacy-free garbling), or using
  public-key primitives.
- Whole-circuit schemes such as MPC-PAPER-2026-LS-GARBLING, which batch layers
  and use non-projective input encodings outside the single-gate interface;
  they neither refute the single-gate bound nor follow from it.

sections.heading: Formal target
sections.content:
A single-gate garbling scheme receives the two input wire label pairs and
outputs a garbled gate and the output labels, for AND gates with input and
output bit flips. All labels have \( \lambda \) bits and share one global
free-XOR offset. Security is the ordinary simulation-based garbling notion
against computationally unbounded adversaries making polynomially many queries
to a random oracle; the evaluator may query adaptively and without coordination.
Decide whether every such scheme satisfies

\[
|\text{garbled gate}| \;\ge\; 1.5\lambda - \mathrm{negl}(\lambda),
\]

either by a proof or by a secure scheme in exactly this model that violates
the bound.

sections.heading: Known obstacles
sections.content:
Within its query model, MPC-PAPER-2025-JRR-GARBLING-BOUNDS already rules out
smaller strongly secure gates, so a smaller construction must escape at least
one of its restrictions. Changing label correlations can give smaller isolated
gates but loses composition, and whole-circuit amortization is a different
problem; neither is evidence about the single-gate bound itself.

sections.heading: Research history
sections.content:
Free XOR made XOR gates cost nothing (MPC-PAPER-2008-FREEXOR).
MPC-PAPER-2015-HALFGATES reached two ciphertexts per AND gate, proved this
optimal among linear schemes, and left lower bounds for arbitrary schemes open.
MPC-PAPER-2021-THREE-HALVES escaped the linear model with slicing and dicing,
reaching \( 1.5\lambda + 5 \) bits, and asked whether this is optimal in
Minicrypt. MPC-PAPER-2025-JRR-GARBLING-BOUNDS proved a matching bound under
query restrictions. MPC-PAPER-2026-LS-GARBLING showed that whole circuits can go
below \( |C|\kappa \) bits by batching layers, a different interface that leaves
the single-gate question as it was.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
Prove the \( 1.5\lambda - \mathrm{negl}(\lambda) \) bound for strongly secure
free-XOR single-gate schemes whose evaluator makes non-adaptive oracle queries
and knows which other input combinations share each query.

sections.heading: Resolution
sections.content:
MPC-PAPER-2025-JRR-GARBLING-BOUNDS models a garbling scheme as a joint
distribution over wire labels, garbled-gate data and oracle answers, derives
Shannon-type inequalities from correctness and strong security, and uses an
automated prover to obtain the bound for AND gates with input and output bit
flips. It matches the \( 1.5\lambda + 5 \) bits of MPC-PAPER-2021-THREE-HALVES
up to lower-order terms. For gates without free XOR, the paper proves under the
same restrictions that an AND gate needs \( 2\lambda \) bits and an XOR gate
\( \lambda \) bits.

named_open_by.statement: Leaves open whether an optimally fair three-party protocol exists without the polylogarithmic factor, and whether fair coin flipping is possible for more than three parties against any number of corruptions.
Calls finding the optimal bias of coin flipping with more than two parties the main open question of the area, and notes that for more than three parties the gap to the lower bound is still large.

related.reason: Coin flipping is the basic function that cannot be computed with complete fairness; the characterization asks which functions can.

metadata.resolution_condition: For every constant n >= 3, a protocol family assuming oblivious transfer (or a weaker assumption) such that for every r the r-round n-party protocol has honest parties output a common bit and every efficient malicious adversary corrupting up to n - 1 parties biases that bit by at most c_n/r plus a negligible term, with c_n depending only on n. Alternatively, a proof that for some constant n every r-round protocol has bias omega(1/r) settles the question negatively.

related_resolved.title: Characterizing two-party functions computable with complete fairness
related_resolved.reason: Coin flipping is the basic function that cannot be computed with complete fairness; the characterization asks which functions can.

sections.heading: Background
sections.content:
In coin flipping the parties jointly output a common random bit, and a
protocol has bias \( \varepsilon \) if no efficient adversary controlling the
corrupted parties can move the probability that the honest parties output 1 by
more than \( \varepsilon \). When at least half of the parties may be
corrupted, MPC-PAPER-1986-CLEVE shows that every r-round protocol has bias
\( \Omega(1/r) \), so coin flipping cannot be computed with complete fairness.
MPC-PAPER-2009-MNS matched this bound for two parties, and how close
protocols for more parties can come to it is the basic quantitative question
about fairness without an honest majority.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
Fix a constant number \( n \ge 3 \) of parties connected by a broadcast channel,
and assume oblivious transfer. Is there, for every number of rounds r, an
r-round coin-flipping protocol whose bias against every efficient malicious
adversary corrupting up to \( n-1 \) parties is \( O(1/r) \), where the
constant may depend on n? A proof that some constant n forces bias
\( \omega(1/r) \) would also settle the question.

sections.heading: Why it is open
sections.content:
The threshold-round protocols of MPC-PAPER-2009-MNS reach \( O(1/r) \) for two
parties and, in MPC-PAPER-2010-BOO, for [fewer than two-thirds
corrupted](MPC-OP-020), but their bias grows doubly exponentially in the gap
between corrupted and honest parties and gives nothing once two thirds or more
are corrupted. Variants of the majority protocol come [within a
polylogarithmic factor of optimal](MPC-OP-022) only for three parties
(MPC-PAPER-2014-HT, MPC-PAPER-2017-BHLT) and for fewer than three quarters
corrupted (MPC-PAPER-2016-AO). For four or more parties against all but one
corrupted, the best bias for constant n is about \( r^{-1/2-\Theta(1)} \)
(MPC-PAPER-2017-BHLT). Even [the three-party case](MPC-OP-021) is open:
MPC-PAPER-2017-BHLT leaves a factor \( \sqrt{\log r} \) and asks whether it is
needed.

sections.heading: What would not resolve it
sections.content:
- Bias \( O(\mathrm{polylog}(r)/r) \), or any bound with a factor that grows
  with r.
- Protocols that tolerate fewer than \( n-1 \) corruptions for some n, or that
  assume an honest majority, where fully secure computation gives an unbiased
  coin.
- Results for a number of parties that grows with r: MPC-PAPER-2018-BHMO shows
  that bias about \( 1/\sqrt{r} \) is unavoidable once n is polynomial in r,
  which says nothing about constant n.

sections.heading: Formal target
sections.content:
Fix a constant n, a synchronous network with a broadcast channel, and a static
malicious adversary corrupting any set of at most \( n-1 \) parties; no
trusted setup, and oblivious transfer may be assumed. The protocol runs r
rounds, and the honest parties always output a common bit, even if corrupted
parties abort. With \( b \) that bit, require for every efficient adversary

\[
\bigl|\Pr[b = 1] - \tfrac12\bigr| \;\le\; \frac{c_n}{r} + \mathrm{negl}(\kappa)
\]

for every r, where \( c_n \) depends only on n.

sections.heading: Known obstacles
sections.content:
The threshold-round technique pays a factor doubly exponential in the gap
between corrupted and honest parties (MPC-PAPER-2010-BOO), and the
majority-protocol variants lose a factor that grows with r. For many parties
the gap is real: MPC-PAPER-2018-BHMO proves bias
\( \tilde\Omega(1/\sqrt{r}) \) when n is polynomial in r, and notes that for
between about \( \log\log r \) and \( \log r \) parties only the
\( \Omega(1/r) \) bound is known. These are limits of known techniques or of
other regimes, not a lower bound for constant n.

sections.heading: Research history
sections.content:
MPC-PAPER-1986-CLEVE proved the \( \Omega(1/r) \) bound, and for more than two
decades the best protocols had bias about \( t/\sqrt{r} \) for t corrupted
parties. MPC-PAPER-2009-MNS reached \( O(1/r) \) for two parties, and
MPC-PAPER-2010-BOO extended it to fewer than two-thirds corrupted.
MPC-PAPER-2014-HT gave the first three-party protocol within a polylogarithmic
factor, MPC-PAPER-2016-AO extended this to fewer than three quarters corrupted,
and MPC-PAPER-2017-BHLT improved the three-party bias to
\( O(\sqrt{\log r}/r) \) and gave \( r^{-1/2-\Theta(1)} \) for every constant
number of parties. MPC-PAPER-2018-BHMO showed that for many parties bias near
\( 1/\sqrt{r} \) is unavoidable.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
Give, for every r, an r-round two-party coin-flipping protocol in which a
malicious party biases the honest party's output by \( O(1/r) \).

sections.heading: Resolution
sections.content:
MPC-PAPER-2009-MNS gives such a protocol assuming oblivious transfer, with
bias at most \( 1/(4r-c) \) for a constant c. Since MPC-PAPER-1986-CLEVE
shows bias at least \( 1/(8r+2) \), the \( \Omega(1/r) \) bound is tight for
two parties, up to a factor of about two; earlier protocols had bias about
\( 1/\sqrt{r} \). The output is fixed at a secret, uniformly chosen
round, before which each party's backup outputs are independent random bits.
MPC-PAPER-2014-HT (§1) describes it as a threshold-round protocol, the
approach that MPC-PAPER-2010-BOO extends to more parties.

metadata.caveat: MPC-PAPER-2010-BOO states its theorem under enhanced trapdoor permutations, which it uses to implement the functionalities its protocol calls, and does not say whether oblivious transfer suffices.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
For a constant number n of parties of which fewer than \( 2n/3 \) are
corrupted, give for every r an r-round coin-flipping protocol with bias
\( O(1/r) \).

sections.heading: Resolution
sections.content:
MPC-PAPER-2010-BOO extends the two-party protocol of MPC-PAPER-2009-MNS to this
setting, assuming enhanced trapdoor permutations and a broadcast channel. With
\( t = (n+k)/2 \) corrupted parties, \( n/2 \le t < 2n/3 \), its r-round
protocol has bias \( O(2^{2^{k+1}}/r') \) with \( r' = r - O(k+1) \), so for
a constant number of parties, or when t exceeds \( n/2 \) by a constant, the
bias is the optimal \( O(1/r) \). MPC-PAPER-2016-AO and MPC-PAPER-2018-BHMO
quote the bound as \( O(2^{2^k}/r) \); both forms grow doubly exponentially
in the gap k between corrupted and honest parties.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
With three parties, any two of which may be corrupted, is there for every r an
r-round coin-flipping protocol with bias \( O(1/r) \)?

sections.heading: Why it is open
sections.content:
Two corrupted parties out of three are two thirds, exactly where the
threshold-round protocols of MPC-PAPER-2010-BOO stop applying.
MPC-PAPER-2014-HT reached bias \( O(\log^3 r/r) \) with a variant of the
majority protocol, and MPC-PAPER-2017-BHLT tightened the analysis to
\( O(\sqrt{\log r}/r) \), so [bias within a polylogarithmic
factor](MPC-OP-023) is settled. Both papers leave open whether the remaining
factor can be removed, and no lower bound above \( \Omega(1/r) \) is known for
three parties.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
For every constant number n of parties and up to \( n-1 \) corruptions, is
there an r-round coin-flipping protocol with bias
\( O(\mathrm{polylog}(r)/r) \)?

sections.heading: Why it is open
sections.content:
Bias within a polylogarithmic factor is known for [three
parties](MPC-OP-023) and for [fewer than three quarters
corrupted](MPC-OP-024). With four or more parties and all but one corrupted,
the best known bias for constant n is [polynomially above
optimal](MPC-OP-025), about \( r^{-1/2-\Theta(1)} \), and MPC-PAPER-2017-BHLT notes that for
more than three parties the gap to the lower bound is still large.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
With three parties, any two of which may be corrupted, give for every r an
r-round coin-flipping protocol with bias \( O(\mathrm{polylog}(r)/r) \).

sections.heading: Resolution
sections.content:
MPC-PAPER-2014-HT proves, assuming oblivious transfer, that for every r there
is an r-round three-party protocol with bias \( O(\log^3 r/r) \) against one
or two corrupted parties; before it, the best bias for two corrupted parties
out of three was about \( 1/\sqrt{r} \). The protocol is a variant of the
majority protocol rather than a threshold-round protocol.
MPC-PAPER-2017-BHLT improves the bias to \( O(\sqrt{\log r}/r) \).

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
For a constant number n of parties of which fewer than \( 3n/4 \) are
corrupted, give for every r an r-round coin-flipping protocol with bias
\( O(\mathrm{polylog}(r)/r) \).

sections.heading: Resolution
sections.content:
MPC-PAPER-2016-AO proves, assuming oblivious transfer, that for constants n
and \( t < 3n/4 \) there is an r-round protocol with bias
\( O(2^{2^n}\log^3 r/r) \) against t corrupted parties, which is
\( O(\log^3 r/r) \) for a constant number of parties. It uses the
secret-sharing technique of MPC-PAPER-2010-BOO to reduce the problem to the
constructions of MPC-PAPER-2014-HT. Before it, protocols for two thirds or more
corrupted parties had bias about \( 1/\sqrt{r} \). The factor
\( 2^{2^n} \), doubly exponential in the number of parties, is why n must be
constant.

profile.Setting: any constant number n of parties, up to n − 1 corrupted

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
For every constant number n of parties and up to \( n-1 \) corruptions, give an
r-round coin-flipping protocol whose bias is \( r^{-1/2-c_n} \) for some
constant \( c_n > 0 \), beating the \( O(n/\sqrt{r}) \) bias of the majority
protocol.

sections.heading: Resolution
sections.content:
MPC-PAPER-2017-BHLT proves, assuming oblivious transfer, that for t parties with
\( t \le \frac12\log\log r \) there is an r-round protocol tolerating up to
\( t-1 \) corrupted parties with bias

\[
O\!\left(\frac{t^4\, 2^t \sqrt{\log r}}{r^{1/2 + 1/(2^{t-1}-2)}}\right),
\]

so \( r^{-1/2-\Theta(1)} \) for a constant number of parties. For three parties
the exponent is 1, which gives the near-optimal three-party bias, but for four
or more parties the bound is polynomially above \( 1/r \).

sections.heading: Background
sections.content:
Complete fairness requires that if one party learns the output, so does the
other. MPC-PAPER-1986-CLEVE implies that without an honest majority some
functions, such as coin flipping and XOR, cannot be computed fairly, and for
two decades no non-trivial two-party function was believed to be fair.
MPC-PAPER-2008-GHKL showed that many are, including AND, OR and the
millionaires' problem, which raised the question of exactly which two-party
functions admit complete fairness.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
Consider two parties, one of which may be maliciously corrupted, and assume
oblivious transfer. Give a necessary and sufficient condition, decidable from
the function's table, for a deterministic function
\( f : X \times Y \to Z_1 \times Z_2 \) with finite domains and finite ranges,
where each party receives its own output, to be computable with full security,
including complete fairness.

sections.heading: Why it is open
sections.content:
MPC-PAPER-2015-ABMO settled [Boolean functions whose two outputs
coincide](MPC-OP-028) with a criterion on the affine span of the rows and
columns of the function's matrix, but for [Boolean functions whose outputs may
differ](MPC-OP-027) its sufficient and necessary conditions leave a gap. For
non-Boolean outputs, MPC-PAPER-2014-ASHAROV shows that some functions over
every finite range are fair, and MPC-PAPER-2017-DM gives tools for designing
fully secure protocols for every constant-domain function, but no condition is
known that is both necessary and sufficient. The known protocols build on the
protocol of MPC-PAPER-2008-GHKL, whose threshold-round structure
MPC-PAPER-2017-DM generalizes, and their reach has been matched by an
impossibility result only for common Boolean outputs.

sections.heading: What would not resolve it
sections.content:
- Fair protocols for further functions or classes without a matching
  impossibility result, or impossibility results without matching protocols.
- Characterizations under relaxed notions such as partial fairness, or with an
  honest majority, where every function can be computed fairly.
- Multiparty characterizations, such as that of MPC-PAPER-2015-ABMO for Boolean
  functions with a constant, even number of parties of which at most half are
  corrupted; they concern a different setting.

sections.heading: Research history
sections.content:
MPC-PAPER-1986-CLEVE ruled out fair coin flipping without an honest majority.
MPC-PAPER-2008-GHKL showed that every function over polynomial-size domains
without an embedded XOR is fair, and that some functions with an embedded XOR
are fair only with super-logarithmically many rounds. MPC-PAPER-2014-ASHAROV
showed that almost all Boolean functions whose two domains differ in size are
fair and extended feasibility to asymmetric and non-Boolean outputs.
MPC-PAPER-2015-ABMO characterized symmetric Boolean functions, and
MPC-PAPER-2017-DM generalized the protocol design to constant-domain functions
while noting that the characterization remains open. For more parties,
MPC-PAPER-2010-FAIR gave the first completely fair multiparty protocols for
non-trivial functions.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
Characterize the deterministic two-party functions with finite domains in which
each party receives one output bit, possibly different from the other's, that
can be computed with complete fairness against one malicious party.

sections.heading: Why it is open
sections.content:
When both parties receive the same bit, MPC-PAPER-2015-ABMO gives [a complete
characterization](MPC-OP-028). For differing output bits it proves a
sufficient condition, generalizing its symmetric protocol, and a necessary
condition, and shows by a new protocol that one function between them is fair;
it states that classifying the remaining functions in the gap is open. MPC-PAPER-2014-ASHAROV first showed that some
asymmetric functions are fair. MPC-PAPER-2017-DM gives an algorithm that,
for a function in this class, either designs a fully secure protocol or fails,
and with it proves fair a function that MPC-PAPER-2015-ABMO had posed as open.
The algorithm also fails on some functions that the known necessary condition
does not rule out, and their status is unknown.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
Characterize the two-party functions with finite domains and one output bit,
the same for both parties, that can be computed with complete fairness against
one malicious party.

sections.heading: Resolution
sections.content:
MPC-PAPER-2015-ABMO proves, assuming oblivious transfer, that such a function,
deterministic or randomized, is computable with complete fairness if and only
if the all-one vector or the all-zero vector lies in the affine span of the
rows or of the columns of its matrix. Every function meeting the condition is
computed with full security by a variant of the protocol of
MPC-PAPER-2008-GHKL. Every other function is semi-balanced, and for those the
impossibility comes from an earlier reduction to fair sampling. This answers,
for this class, the question that MPC-PAPER-2008-GHKL left open.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
Decide which two-party functions with a common output bit and no embedded XOR,
that is, with no inputs \( x_0, x_1, y_0, y_1 \) such that
\( f(x_i, y_j) = i \oplus j \), can be computed with complete fairness against
one malicious party.

sections.heading: Resolution
sections.content:
MPC-PAPER-2008-GHKL shows, assuming enhanced trapdoor permutations, that every
function over polynomial-size domains without an embedded XOR can be computed
with complete fairness, so all of them are fair; it notes that oblivious
transfer is necessary and sufficient for this result. The protocol reduces each
such function to the greater-than function and takes a number of rounds linear
in the domain size. The class includes AND, OR and Yao's millionaires' problem.
This was the first evidence that non-trivial functions escape the
impossibility of MPC-PAPER-1986-CLEVE.
